I should like to draw the attention of the Government to this despatch which appears in this morning's Citizen, under date of Winnipeg, April 24:
The Manitoba court of appeal to-day delivered judgment in the stated case of The King versus the Manitoba Grain Company, declaring section 215 of the Canada Grain Act ultra vires of the federal parliament. This section of the act stated that ''no person shall engage in the business of selling grain on commission or receive or solicit consignments of grain for sale on commission, in the western inspection division, without first obtaining such annual license from the board.
The appeal arose from a conviction registered in the provincial police court last year, when Magistrate OR. M. Noble fined the Manitoba Grain Company $500 for selling grain without a license. The case has aroused considerable interest owing to the fact that the validity of the Canada Grain Act was attacked by counsel for the defendant company. At the time of the conviction Magistrate Noble granted a stated case.
In this connection I should like to ask the Government what action it intends to take in this matter in order that producers of grain may be protected from the many

Supply-Railways
mushroom grain companies which will inevitably spring up now that sections of the Canada Grain Act are held to be ultra vires.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. C. KENNEDY (Essex, Minister of Railways and Canals) :
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There is very little, if any, change as compared with last year. The vote is less and the number of employees fewer than was the case last year; but I may say, in justice to my predecessor, that this reduction was made before I took charge in January last. During the time I have been in office there have been no new appointments. There are two vacancies, one caused by death and the other by resignation. The increases in vote are statutory, and the change in the designation of certain em-
Supply-Railways

ployees is the result of the reclassification. When I took charge I told the deputy minister that I was anxious that we should have efficiency, first of all, but with that efficiency we should economize as far as possible. I believe that these estimates have been prepared with that end in view. As we proceed I shall be glad to give any explanations that may be required.

There are four increases in salaries to the higher-paid officials of this department, three increases of $180 each and one of $300. As the minister says, these are statutory increases, but I desire to make an observation with reference to the salaries of the higher-paid officials. In the consideration of civil government estimates for some of the other departments, the opinion was expressed, from both groups on this side of the House, that, having regard to the general tendency towards deflation, the salaries of the higher-paid officials might very well be left on the basis of 1921. 'In connection with this department, in regard to which I have some little knowledge, I think that if the higher-paid officials had directed their unquestioned talents to private and corporate interests with the same devotion as they have applied themselves to the public service, they would be in receipt of very much larger salaries than are provided in these estimates. I entirely support the vote under consideration.
I have no intention of precipitating any general discussion on the railway situation under this vote, as I understand it to be the custom, under the civil government vote, to confine the discussion exclusively to matters of civil government, the general policy with regard to the railways being discussed on the general estimates. But I want to ask the minister a question which, I think, is pertinent, even at this time. The Toronto Globe has been for so long a time intimately associated with the Liberal party and its policies that, in Ontario at least, an editorial statement by that journal is taken as carrying almost the same force as an expression of government policy when the Liberal party is in power. I wish to refer to the leading editorial in the Globe of yesterday. That editorial, dealing with the question of the National Railways, contains two statements:
The Globe believes there are big enough men in the ranks of Canada's railway operators to carry the national system to success, and that Mr. Kennedy will discover and make use

of their talents. Some of them will doubtless be found in the service of the Canadian National and the Grand Trunk; some may even be drawn from the Canadian Pacific.
Further on it says:
In the end, perhaps, it may be found that there is room within the National System for the C.P.R. itself on terms that will be equitable alike to its shareholders and to the public.
The question I would ask the minister is, does the editorial in the Globe reflect the policy of the Government? Is the policy of the Government in accord with that editorial; or is that editorial intended as a feeler to test public opinion in reference to this important matter?

Like everyone else in the province of Ontario who reads the Globe, I pay considerable attention to its editorials, and I had the pleasure of reading the editorials in question. My hon. friend, as a former minister of this department, knows that the minister is also receiving suggestions as to what he should do in railway matters. The Globe, I suppose, has, like many other papers, kindly made suggestions. Beyond that I do not know anything about the editorial. I would say that it reflects simply the ideas of the editor. As to its reflecting the policy of the Government, I have no doubt that the Government will lay down its own policy when the right time comes.
The right-of-way agent is Mr. Fraser, I believe. Is he confining his duties to the old National railways, or is he right-of-way agent for the whole system?
He is the departmental right-of-way agent and does work in the East that may be necessary for the department and for the railways also.

My excuse for asking the minister a question which would more naturally be considered under the main estimates is that it would relieve considerable anxiety on the part of a number of my constituents if I could have some assurance from him that the pronouncement he made When [DOT]these estimates were last under discussion, that no new rails would be laid this year, is not, like the laws of Modes and Persians, entirely unchangeable. I have in mind, Sir, that road of which I have no doubt you have some knowledge-the branch line running from Kamloops to Kelowna through the Okanagan Valley. That road has been practically completed for two years so far as the grade is concerned, at an ex-

Supply-Militia
penditure of five million dollars, involving, of course, a very heavy annual charge for interest, while the depreciation on the roadbed at a conservative estimate must amount to 20 per cent per annum. Good and ample justification could be given for the completion of that line this summer in order that it may be ready to handle this season's fruit and vegetable crops. This road would be second to no other branch line as a feeder for the National railways, and the minister will, I am sure, agree that our National railway system stands very much in need of additional business. The latest figures I have available are for 1919, when from three stations in that district, Armstrong, Vernon, and Kelowna, 320 full cars of fruit and vegetables were shipped and 165,000 odd packages of express; in addition there were shipments of live stock, hay and other products. One section of that line passes through the Salmon river district in which lies probably the most valuable gypsum deposits in the world; they are practically one hundred per cent pure.
Order. I would draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that this subject hardly comes under "Civil Government."

I was going to crave the indulgence of yourself, Mr. Chairman, and the minister, for the reason I gave at the outset. I am deluged with telegrams and resolutions from the local Boards of Trade asking for an immediate response, and if the minister could give some assurance to allay their anxiety I should be much obliged. He has a reputation, well earned I am sure, of being a thorough business man.. For business reasons alone the outlay necessary to complete this line could be amply justified.

Like my hon. friend, I have had many representations in connection with this particular line. But may I say to him that his district is not alone in making representations for railway accommodation? From all parts of the West I have had similar representations of their transportation needs. The policy of the Government in respect to the laying of new lines this year is simply this: We felt that, the new board coming in, the responsibility for any capital expenditure should properly belong to that board, and that for the time being, until they have had an opportunity of ascertaining whether the expenditure would be warranted, we should not go on with any new
work. However, we are impressed with the necessity of doing something in the district my hon. friend has mentioned, and I can promise him that when the new board is appointed every consideration will be given to the matter.

Just a moment, Mr. Chairman. I think some of us heard the word "carried " before we got to the page. This is rather too important an item to be carried without any discussion whatever, and we would like a statement from the minister in reference to it.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence) : I hardly expected it to go through so rapidly as that.
You are quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The militia estimates,
I might say, have been pared down to a point as low as is compatible with national safety; in fact, I have been criticized quite severely for some of the reductions. I think it is well that Parliament should discuss this question. Our militia force was not a mushroom or accidental growth, it took a good many years of development before Canada became of sufficient importance and exercised autonomy to such a marked degree that she undertook her own militia defence. The matter was discussed in the Imperial Parliament on several occasions, and it is a well-known fact that not a few of the members of the British House of Commons and some members of the British cabinet opposed Canada being allowed-if I may put it in that form-to have, control of her militia, because it was feared that it would tend to encourage the idea of too great independence and would weaken the tie that binds us to the Motherland. That fear, of course, has been dispelled, because the principle enunciated by Lord Grey as far back as 1851 has been fully borne out by our subsequent history, namely, that the greater the responsibility you place on what might be called the subordinate body, the stronger becomes its attachment to the head. So it has been with the Dominion, as year by year she has developed, greater responsibility has been placed upon her to manage her own affairs, and instead of the tie that binds us to the Motherland being weakened, that
Supply-Militia

Why is the principal
reduction in these estimates confined to the permanent force?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The reduction will not
interfere materially with the efficiency of the force, being in large measure among officers and non-commissioned officers, under a rearrangement that the chief of staff proposes to make.
Does the hon. minister say that the reduction in' the noncommissioned officers will be a move towards efficiency?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would not like to go
so far as that. My hon. friend is a military man, and he is confronting me with a technique that I am not familiar with. It would be a reduction of the units in various parts of the Dominion, and a rearrangement under a new plan. As I was pointing out, now that we have assumed the status of a nation we must carry on those departments which are incident to that status. Hon. gentlemen have said to

Supp ly-M ilitia
me: Why spend money on the militia, seeing that it is non-productive? I reply: Why spend money on fire insurance when it is non-productive? Let there be disorder in any part of the Dominion that the Militia Department is unable to cope with, and immediately we would be criticized because we were unprepared to meet the emergency. Could we, Mr. Chairman, let it be known throughout the entire world that Canada is a country where the militia is ineffective, where the mounted police is to be reduced almost to the vanishing point, where the naval service is to be of little account, and where the flying force is not to function? We would become the mecca of a class of people that would not be desirable in the best interests of the country. It is our duty, even though the militia be not productive, to maintain it at sufficient strength to preserve order and good government within the Dominion. The militia is not productive, but it is highly protective, and if it were not for this force Canada would not be in the position she occupies to-day.
I wanted to make these few observations because as a nation we are at the present time looking forward to standing side by side with the other nations of the world. If we are to realize our aspirations, we must accept the responsibilities that go with those aspirations and be prepared to carry on our share of defence work as part of the British Empire, and that share, so far as the militia is concerned, is provided for in the estimates I am now presenting.

Does the minister mean that he is going to increase the militia expenditure in this country under present conditions, when people want to get back to a peace basis and are desirous that the militia should be cut down practically to an infinitesimal point?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The estimates are not being increased; they are being decreased. So far as the amount is concerned; if we compare this year with 1913-1914, when we were on a peace basis, the estimates this year are less; and if you take into account the present purchasing power of the dollar as compared with 1911-1912, I submit the estimates presented to-day are less than they were that year.
I congratulate the minister on that.
What is the reduction in the number of men in the permanent force?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The estimate made by the department and the Chief of Staff is
that when the reorganization is completed the reduction will be in the vicinity of 400 or 500 all told.
But this vote shows an increase of about $100,000 over last year for clothing and necessaries. How does the minister account for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I might point out to the hon. member that there are two branches of the force, the permanent force and the volunteers. The $100,000 which my hon. friend mentions is for the volunteer force, which is not, strictly speaking, the militia.
Is the volunteer force larger this year than last?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is exactly the same, but we have reduced the amount for annual drill by $100,000. There is also this to be taken into consideration. After the war there was a good deal of clothing on hand, but as that is used up more is required. More clothing may be required in certain lines one year than another. For instance, we have stocks on hand now of certain lines, but in other lines our stock is diminishing.
The expenditure for 1919-1920 for cadet service was $390,000 and to-day it is $450,000. What is the explanation of the increase?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We have not come to that item yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not averse to discussing all the items now, but answering first my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), if he will look at the increase he suggested in the item for clothing and necessaries, he will find that it is merely a cross-entry, a simple matter of bookkeeping. It is a decrease in war-like stores, transferred from one account to the other.

I want to congratulate the minister for having made a reduction in the estimates as compared with last year.
I think he is entitled to some credit for giving us this evidence of economy on the part of his department. At the same time it is only fair to say that I have an objection to register, and it is that the reduction is not sufficient. Without going into details of these items, which I presume will be taken up separately, I should like for a moment to compare the estimates of this department with the amount of less than $5,000,000 asked for by the Department of Agriculture, which is the fundamental and basic industry of this country. I know very well that you cannot always very
Su pp ly-M ilitia

reasonably compare these estimates under the circumstances. But take the estimates of other departments of the Government.
I find that the Health Department, for instance, is asking something under $1,000,000; Administration of Justice, slightly over $2,000,000; Immigration and Colonization, slightly over $2,000,000,-and I think no one will under-estimate the value and significance of the work for which that estimate is being asked,-Fisheries, slightly over $1,000,000; Mines, slightly over $500,000; Labour Department, the main estimates for which are something under $1,500,000; Dominion Lands and Parks, almost $5,000,000; Soldiers' Land Settlement, approximately $12,000,000; and finally, may I just mention the estimates for the Department of Trade and Commerce which total slightly over $3,000,000. I think in comparison with these other necessary and fundamental departments of government, the estimate for the Militia Department is out of all proportion. I realize, of course, the necessity for maintaining in this country not only a militia, but a Militia Department, properly staffed and properly officered, and I have nothing to say with regard to the efficiency and effectiveness of our miltia. I think perhaps it is true, as the minister has stated, that the militia generally has served satisfactorily; but I do think in view of the estimates for other departments of government, there should be a very substantial reduction in the militia estimates, especially as we have just come through a long war, and have had a conference at Washington on the limitation of armaments, and particularly in view of the very difficult economic conditions that prevail throughout this country. I do not propose to move any amendment, but I want to urge upon the minister the necessity for doing something far more substantial than he has done in reducing the estimates of his department.

I should like to say a word on the question of the total amount which the minister is asking for on this occasion, and the remarks which have fallen from my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), that they show a substantial decrease from the vote of last year.
The vote of last year was $11,954,000, and the total expenditure until 31st March this year, I think I am safe in saying, was under $10,250,000. I have not received the figures yet, but from my knowledge of the department up till the end of December and from estimates I have been able to make

since, I think I am within the mark when I say that $10,250,000 will cover every dollar that was spent last year. This year it is proposed to expend $10,788,000. So the reduction is rather more apparent than real, is it not, Mr. Chairman? However, under all the circumstances which we have in Canada to-day, if we are going to maintain a militia force in this country that is to be of any practical use, I do not believe that the minister can cut very much below the figure he has submitted to the House on the present occasion. I am inclined to think that in some instances his figures are too low; in some others perhaps they may be slightly too high. But it is not correct to say that Canada is one of the nations which is engaged in extravagant military expenditure. I went to some pains just a year ago to make a comparison as between Canada and every other country in the world, just to see what we were spending and how our expenditure compared with our neighbours. My hon. friends who are inclined to be critical can go to any country on the face of the glohe, civilized or uncivilized, they can inquire in Europe, in Asia, in America North or South, and they will find that comparison shows that Canada is a long way below the lowest of them in all classes of expenditure on armaments-so far below the lowest that one is almost ashamed to make the comparison. These figures were all submitted by experts to a Financial Conference held in Brussels in October, 1921. The figures are accurate, they were submitted as a result of a call by the League of Nations; and in every comparison you make, the expenditure in this country for military purposes is almost nothing as compared with similar expenditure by our nearest neighbour whether it be a British Dominion or whether it be an independent country. The charge that we are extravagant in this respect, is entirely unfounded, if you compare our expenditure with what any other nation in the world is doing. Now, I submit that the minister has cut these estimates to just about as low a figure as he can go. There may be some details, perhaps, that will stand some paring down; but on the whole I doubt very much if he can go any lower without actually injuring the service.

Are there not many
things in connection with the Militia Department that could be dispensed with in view of other public services being starved?

Supply-Militia

I do not know about
any public services that are being starved, but the point I make is this: If it is the wisdom of this House that we should maintain in Canada a reasonable militia force as was done in the past, if it is the judgment of the House that we should have a militia force at all, then you cannot pay much less than the minister proposes to pay for it this year. On the other hand, if in the judgment of the House the force should be wiped out then he could save that money and apply it to something else. You cannot have your cake and eat it,-if you are going to have a force, and if this force is to be an efficient one, it is going to cost you what the minister is asking for.

What is the wisdom
of permitting drill halls to be lit up all through the winter months and having parades there in order that officers may display their gold braid, while people are starving in this country?

I think, Mr. Chairman, with your permission and that of the minister it might be as well to allow us to deal with the whole series of items connected with this subject instead of limiting the discussion to one item alone. I think that has been the usual practice in previous years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The items all form
separate resolutions, I am sorry to say.

I think that would be the quickest way-to deal with the entire vote. I also would like to congratulate the minister upon reducing the total estimate from something over $11,954,000 to $10,788,000; but I would like to say that I think, in the present condition of affairs in Canada, in future this expenditure can be greatly reduced. Of course the Minister of Militia has only been in charge of this department for some three months and it was impossible for him in that time to consult the excellent staff of officials he has surrounding him in the department, to discuss matters thoroughly with them, and get such a grasp of affairs, that he could, in respect to a number of the militia items, curtail the expenditure. But the people of Canada are expecting the Minister of Militia to do that in the next twelve months, so that when he presents his estimates to Parliament in 1923 he may make it manifest that those estimates have been cut to the fullest extent compatible with the best interests of the country. I agree with the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and with the minister too, that it is necessary to have a militia force in Canada, but it seems to me that that force should be managed as economically as possible. I believe it is possible to have a skeleton organization;
4 p.m. I do not think it is necessary to spend some of the large amounts which are being expended in connection with this department. Undoubtedly it is necessary in different sections of Canada to maintain such units or organizations that if it were necessary, owing to trouble, to call out the .volunteers the needed personnel for taking charge of these units would be available; but I do nofr think it is necessary to spend large sums of money in connection with the militia. The people of Canada irrespective of politics will support what the hon. member for Calgary has said in this regard. I believe too that the people will back up any government or any party that will cut to the lowest possible point not only the militia expenditure but the so-called naval expenditure, which latter is absolutely a waste of public money. I am not criticising the present minister, for he has only been in charge of the Militia Department for three months, but I would like to call his attention to one item. I do not wish to ask the minister to reduce his estimates by resolution of this committee. I have a great deal of faith in the minister and some of his officials; they have the best interest of the country at heart just as much as my hon. friend from Calgary or any other member, and although the item to which I am about to refer appears in the estimates I do not think the minister will spend one dollar of that money during the coming season. The item to which I refer is Annual Drill, $1,400,000. The minister and his officials have already shown their good intentions by cutting this item down from $1,500,000 as it was last year to $1,400,000 this year.- The mere fact that this item appears in the estimates does not mean that there is any necessity for its expenditure. The hon. member for South Wellington, who was minister of militia in the National Liberal and Conservative Government, told us a few moments ago -and I presume that in so doing he was endeavouring to present himself with a bouquet-that, although last year when he was minister the militia estimates called for $11,954,000, they only spent $10,250,000 or thereabouts. Now, Sir, I have such confidence in the present Minister of

Militia that although his estimates call for $10,780,000 it will be a matter of great surprise and disappointment to me if when he comes to present the militia estimates next year he does not show that instead of expending any such sum he has only paid out some six or seven million dollars. Reductions such as that in this expenditure are what the people of this country want. There is one sum that need not be expended this year, as I have already said, and that is $1,400,000 for annual drill.

House would not be violated by his doing so, I should like my hon. friend (Mr. Duff) to conclude his remarks. Suppose we carry the first item, and then he can discuss the first one on the second.

speechtext: I am instructed that it is the rule of the committee that these resolutions should be discussed separately. There may be some items in this resolution, but there is, at present before the committee, one resolution, namely, No. 89, Allowances, Active Militia.

When I was interrupted by the Chair, I was endeavouring to say that the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who was Minister of Militia in the late government, in the remarks which he made a few minutes ago, when he was discussing what he termed reasonable expenditure on the service, compared the total expenditure in Canada with expenditures in other countries. It is quite true that the expenditure for militia purposes in Canada is much smaller by head of population than similar expenditure in any other country; but we must agree that

conditions in Canada are altogether different from conditions in other countries. For instance, nobody in Canada wants to have conditions as they are in Russia to-day. I have read in the newspapers of two or three men in Canada who have said that we should have conditions as they exist in Russia to-day; but I do not belong to that class, and I believe ninety-nine per cent of the people of this country would be strongly opposed to our having conditions as they are in Russia to-day. Furthermore, I do not believe anybody in Canada with any common-sense wants to have conditions as they are in France or in any other European country. Consequently, it is not necessary that the people of Canada should vote for militia purposes such large expenditures as must be made in other countries. Therefore, I do not think that the argument of the hon. member for South Wellington should have very much weight and effect when he says that we should spend large sums of money for militia purposes, because, forsooth, other countries are spending large amounts.
As I said a moment ago, it seems to me that the estimate for annual drill should not be spent this year at least. If ever the necessity arose, we have in this country 400,000 men who are available at any time for service of this kind, in order to maintain peace and order in Canada. It is a well-known fact that during the late war, the men who were gathered in at a few moments' notice and who were outside of the active militia of this country, made the very best soldiers which Canada or the United States or any other country sent to the war. Men who were taken from ordinary avocations in life in this or any other country, after a little training, made as good soldiers as other men who had spent many years in military service. With the available material in this country, if anything happened, we do not need to have a great standing army. I have no objection to the estimate for the permanent force. I notice the minister and his officials have cut down this amount by $755,000. That is a step in the right direction, and the minister should be congratulated that, at this stage in the affairs of Canada, in our present financial and industrial condition, the estimate for the permanent force has been reduced by $755,000. I notice that the item for the Dominion arsenal at Lindsay shows a reduction of $218,300.

Hear, hear.

My hon. friends say "hear, hear." Aill the "hear, hear'b" in the world will not prevent me from giving expression to the views that, as a representative of a constituency in the federal Parliament, I have been sent here to present to this House.
I want, first of all, to congratulate the Minister of Militia and Defence upon the fact that he has, to some extent, decreased the militia estimates. I have every respect for the Minister of Militia and Defence, but I want to assure him that I believe he has taken too much advice from officials in his department who are fonder of gold braid parades than of the interest of the people of this country. It seems to me that, while we require a certain militia in this Dominion, this militia should be reduced to the finest possible point. We have heard ini this House debates about unemployment; we know that agriculture in Canada is being starved; and now, even though this country is in dire straits financially, and whilst the minister-and I congratulate him personally and not his officials upon this fact-has decreased the estimates, this vote for militia is being maintained in order that we shall have in Canada people who, fresh from o'er the seas, give native Canadians the feeling that they are being looked upon with an easy sort of tolerance. These people want to have gold braid matches in order that they may parade before the people of this country their connection with Sir So-and-So and Sir Somebody Else. The people
of Canada do not care whether you have an ancestor, a family tree, or not, so long as you are able to do an honest man's work with brain and hand; and we, in this Dominion, as a young nation, a nation within the British Empire, a nation that has a right to control its own affairs, want the least possible amount of militarism. I pray the indulgence of the minister while I ask him that he be good enough to dto his utmost to see that these estimates are brought down to the lowest possible point.
What do we find as regards militia camps in this Dominion? Some people who go to these camps seem to forget that they are Canadians at all; they seem to assume, during these camps, a sort of autocratic spirit, and the idea is to grind down the young intelligent Canadian, who goes there primarily for instruction that may fit him, if the time ever came, to defend his native land. The minister, if I may be figurative, is on the hilltop listening to the murmurs of the far off sea, but he fails to realize that young men must be fitted to brave the stream of life. He looks upon the distant sea, but he does not note the rushing tide below him. In my opinion the Militia Department of Canada exists to-day for no other purpose than the holding of gold-laced parades. We are asked to spend the sum of $10,788,400 for gold-lace parades and nothing else, while agricultural exhibitions in the country cannot receive any aid from the Department of Agriculture. speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Like the leader of the Opposition, (Mr. Meighen) I do not see that there is much difficulty in the way. I think we can proceed calmly. Each one of the items is an entity in the whole, and in discussing one you can certainly refer to others. The bearing which this item has on the others is discussable. The Chairman is merely trying to avoid any discussion in detail of all the items under one particular vote, and then going over the same items all over again when we take them up in their order. These resolutions have been submitted to His Excellency and must be discussed in their order; but I see no objection to a general discussion of the status of the militia.

Supply-Militia

What I have to
say, Mr. Chairman, concerns not, perhaps, this particular item so much as the underlying principle of the maintenance of any-think like a large force in Canada. Some of us are not in a position to discuss the particular items; it is obvious that one item might be reduced and others left as they are, and that the efficiency of the force might thereby be impaired.
The minister has suggested1-and I think we can all agree-that the time has come when Canada is quite capable of administering her own affairs. The question arises, then, as to the principle on which we propose to administer our affairs. It seems to be taken for granted that we must follow the example of European nations and proceed to arm; in fact, the minister says that we must have all the departments necessary for the equipment of a nation. Now, I should like to challenge the implication that in order that we may become a self-sufficient nation it is necessary for us to maintain a military force. At this particular time we are talking about international disarmament; it would seem that the best way to bring about international disarmament is by national disarmament. We in Canada are in a peculiarly good position to accomplish this. We have the Pacific on the west, the Atlantic on the east; we are bordered by a friendly nation to the south; why should we be prepared to resist aggression on any of these fronts? We have made it a boast that throughout the past century we have had no warships upon the Great Lakes, and we have said that that in itself is the greatest safeguard we have against warfare between the United States and ourselves. What is true in regard to warships on the Great Lakes is equally true in regard to armed forces; we need not seek to protect ourselves against aggression from the south. It may be said that we ought to be prepared to protect ourselves against any unnamed enemy who might arise from some unexpected quarter and seek to injure our nation. I take it, however, there is a growing sentiment on the part of a large number of the Canadian people that since we professed to have gone into the great war to end war, now that the war is over we should try to get back to an absolute peace basis. This Parliament succeeds the one which administered affairs during the period the war was in progress. Now is the time when we should decide whether or not an armed
force means or makes for peace. I for one -and I think I voice the sentiment of a considerable number-have been led to doubt that very much.
It has been further suggested that perhaps we ought to protect ourselves because of probable internal disturbance, I submit that our position in this country is very different from that of European states; we have no subordinate races that must be kept down or are in danger of rising against the nation as a whole, I do not think we have any classes that are particularly dangerous. A good many of our forefathers came here in order to escape the military burdens of Europe; why should we proceed to set up military forces in this country similar to those which they left in Europe? If we provide for the needs of the people, there is no doubt that we shall have a loyal population. Who are we, anyway? We are all anxious to make a living for ourselves, anxious that our families shall have a decent education and so on; that is the feeling of the Canadian people. Under these circumstances, what group is there that we need fear? Now that the war is past we ought to reconsider this whole matter and decide whether we need maintain military forces in this country. Instead of being an insurance against trouble they are rather, it seems to me, provocative of trouble.

After listening to the discussion and after giving the matter some little consideration, it seems to me that the first thing to be done is to decide upon a policy. The first question is, if we want a military force, why do we need it? Do we fear invasion or aggression from any other country? Are we preparing for a war, and if so, against whom? If that is out of the question; if aggression or invasion on the part ol any other country is not to be thought of then should we have an armed force t( preserve internal peace? I think we should, there is no city in the Dominion that does not require a police force, though we are a peaceable people. Then, if we should have a national force, the question is, of what size should that national force be? Having decided that, we can reasonably proceed to have a national force as large as necessary, but no larger. If we are preparing for or expect another war, if we anticipate foreign trouble of any kind at any time in the future, what size of force do we need? It seems to me that these are the questions that should first be
Supply-Militia

settled. 1 do not think we should anticipate any trouble from foreign countries.
I do not think we need fear any aggression on the part of our southern neighbours. We fear no trouble from Europe; we need anticipate no trouble from the Eastern countries across the Pacific. Then the question is-i Come back to it-what size of force is necessary? That we should have some force there is no doubt, but I think the present force is too large for internal purposes, and the general policy should be adopted of cutting it down to the lowest possible point. If the force is maintained1 beyond what is necessary, it is a waste of money, and money is very much needed for other and productive purposes. I shall have a few words to say on the next item- I may not, I suppose, speak on it now, Mr. Chairman-but in my judgment the annual drill is a waste of money. I know it was cut out a few years ago, and I do not think we had the annual drill last year. In any case, it was not general; it may have been held in some places.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This estimate is lower than the one last year.

I know it is, and I think it should1 be lower still. Now, I used to drill some years ago and I know it was just a holiday. While the country was rich and we had money to spend, perhaps there was no great barm in it, but we have not the money to spend now. I know that captains in the militia, in order to make up the full complement of their companies, had to take men much over age, and in the cavalry regiments horses were used that would be no good for war purposes. The men who went to drill looked upon it simply as a holiday. When war actually broke out very few of them were available or of any use. The young men of the country, and middle-aged men too, volunteered in large numbers and made good soldiers, but only a small proportion of the active militia were available or were any good.
It is no good at all.

My hon. friend says that it is no good at all; well, I pretty much agree with that. If there is one item in this appropriation that ought to be cut out it is that which provides for the annual drill-and there may be others.
To summarize what I have said: the first thing to be done is to decide what policy we should pursue, whether we fear, or expect, or anticipate, aggression from any

country within the next few years. If we do not anticipate anything of that kind, then we should not provide for it. We have no money to waste; we have no money to spend on frills.

The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) intimated that we ought to be ashamed of our situation as compared with the situation in some of the European countries. I suggest that we ought rather to be proud of it. In regard to the total figures as indicated in the estimates, I would like to call attention to the fact that a dollar goes a good deal further this year than it did last year, and when allowance is made for that, possibly the comparison between the respective amounts is not as attractive as it might otherwise seem.
I would like to emphasize the sentiments that have already been expressed by several hon. members to the effect that we are spending relatively too much money on the militia. So far as my observation has gone, militia quarters and militia activities are rather in the nature of gold braid and fuss-and-feathers entertainment-a sort of social club-than anything of a strictly protective or military character. I do not say that unkindly or with the idea of reflecting upon any other person who may be connected with the militia. But so far as my observation goes, things tend inevitably that way, and it is not a good way; it does not do the country any good. And occasionally we have exhibitions, that are, to say the least, disgraceful.
In regard to the need for preserving order at home I do think that the member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) is right when he says that we are overstaffed or "over-forced" so far as the militia is concerned. We have had a great deal of talk about unemployment and about unrest, and I think that lurking in some peoples' minds there is a thought that the militia may be necessary in order to put down agitators.- people who are stirring up the unrest which has arisen out of bad industrial or social conditions. Now, let me make this suggestion if $5,000,000 that is voted for militia purposes could be transferred to the solution of the problem of unemployment, we would not need so much miltia and we could have a much happier solution of these labour difficulties and this unrest than we can possibly bring about by maintaining or increasing a force capable of suppressing anything of that nature, I feel very strongly that if that is in our minds at

all, we ought to get rid of it; it is not the right way to handle problems of that sort.
I do believe, of course, in having sufficient police to maintain law and order. But we must not think that we have to have a large and still larger force for that purpose, because difficulties of that type ought to be handled in an altogether different way. I therefore repeat my suggestion that the diversion of a very large part of this vote along other lines would be very much more satisfactory to this country.
As I said a little while ago, a serious difficulty presents itself to any of us who wish to suggest a reduction in the total vote. If we consider the vote item by item, there are few here who understand the details sufficiently to be able to say that this or that particular vote ought to be cut down by such and such an amount. I feel that the total vote ought to be reduced, but I cannot put my finger on any particular item. I suggest that, if it is in order, we should be able at some time during the discussion to move a reduction in the total vote without having to move a reduction in each particular item. Of course, if we go through each item and pass it, we are not then in a position to move any reduction in the total.

I do not believe there is any difference of opinion among the members of the committee on the question whether we ought to maintain a militia in Canada. I do not think any hon. member would move that the militia should be dispensed with. That being the case, it comes down to a question of proportion, a question of quantity. With what has been said on both sides as to the restrictions which should be made effective with regard to our militia expenditure I am in full sympathy, and I would be much more critical of the items on this page of the estimates were we not to have in the near future a reorganization of the Department of Defence, which will mean that the Minister of Defence will have to look into the reorganization of the militia as well. If it were not for that, I would, with many members on both sides of the House, ask the minister not to expend the money that we are going to vote to him. But I do not think it would be wise under the circumstances, either on this item or on the total vote of $10,000,000, to go into the details of where a cut should be made. It is a good thing, I think, that the opinion of so many members has been expressed and that that opinion has been unanimous with 73
regard to the desirability of curtailing militia expenditure and reducing it to the minimum. But some of the items will, I think, bear investigation and in connection with them some hon. members may wish to draw to the attention of the Government the desirability of not expending the total amount voted. I have been connected with the militia for about twenty years now, and I know something about it. During the last ten or twelve years money has been spent foolishly, lavishly, in many centres, and curtailments are , absolutely necessary. For instance, on the staff of each of the various districts the minister has a paymaster, an assistant paymaster and an auditor. Why should there be any necessity for having these three officers in each of the districts? If the paymaster is a responsible officer, no more audit beyond what the Auditor General does and what the General Paymaster does, should be needed. I grant that during the war the volume of business transacted in every district may have justified the appointment of auditors, but the war has been over for three years now, and I think we can dispense with the services of the auditors in the various military districts. That is only one instance. I have asked the minister to give me some information by letter, and I shall have something to say when we come to the item for the general staff. I think that we could dispense with a number of officers who are now employed on the general staff. I pointed out to the minister and the House the other day that we had seventeen generals in Canada to manage the affairs of the militia, whereas ten years ago we could manage the whole business with two or three generals, who were paid between $4,000 and $5,000 each, as compared with between $6,000 and $9,500 which these generals are drawing to-day-* and we have seventeen of them. Yet when the minister, carrying out the policy which now receives the approval of the committee, puts some of these men on the superannuation list, he is criticized by the former Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) and his friends, who almost shed tears on the retirement of these great generals. These generals are being superannuated on a very generous basis indeed. To cite only one case, that of General Burstall, whose name was mentioned the other day, I am told that he is being superannuated on $6,000 a year, which is $2,000 more than the salary he drew in 1914.

More than Mr. Doherty, the ex-Minister of Justice. .

Some of these cases will bear investigation. I would urge upon the department the necessity for further curtailing the list of staff appointments. We have too many generals in Canada; we have too many officers on the permanent staff. I know that it is the intention of the minister, in the reorganization of his department, to bring about this reform, and if we were not on the eve of passing a bill reorganizing the whole defence of Canada I would be much more inquisitive as to the item we are now discussing and much more critical as to the amounts we are asked to vote. We have curtailed the expenditure by $1,000,000, and I am sure that the minister will not expend all of the $10,788,000 which he is asking for. I am in full accord with the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) when he suggests that next year the Minister of Defence, as he will then be called, should be able to come to this House and tell us that instead of expending $10,000,000, he has spent only $8,000,000 or $9,000,000.
