My hon. friend says $5,000,-
000.	That raises the question how much the militia expenditure should be curtailed. If you have a militia you have to give them some training, or you do away with the militia altogether. I would cut down the annual training-and this will probably be one of my suggestions when the item comes up-to a minimum, for a few years to come. We are in no immediate danger of an uprising within this country or of an attack from outside. I think we could take a holiday for a few years in many lines of military activity. So far as that is concerned I wish to support heartily the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Lunenburg and some hon. members on the opposite side of the House, urging the minister in the reorganization of his department to curtail expenditure as much as possible and not to expend the amount which he is now asking for.

where the officers and non-commissioned officers of the militia get their real training in military matters. In view of all I have said I maintain that the expenditure provided in the item under discussion is necessary and I hope it will not be curtailed to any further extent. I believe that the present Minister of Militia, like those who immediately preceded him in that office, is well disposed towards the militia, but I hope he will not proceed too far in the direction of economy and injure the militia beyond repair. While it is necessary to have economy we do not want to carry that policy to an undesirable extreme so far as the militia is concerned, otherwise the force will be simply as it was in the days of 1812 and 1813. If disaster to the militia is contemplated that result will be obtained by adopting the advice of some of the critics whom we have heard this afternoon.

In rising to speak upon this subject I might ask the same question that has been so often heard among our neighbours to the south, "Who won the war?" My hon. friend who has just spoken seems to claim the credit for the militia of Canada, but I am sure there is no hon. member but will acknowledge that it was the laymen-the men picked from the prairies and from the industries in our towns and cities, the men who desired in their hearts to go out and help the Motherland to defeat the common enemy, and not the trained militia who exerted the greatest influence in winning success. The militia wlw had been in training for years were a very slight factor in the winning of the war.
Will my hon. friend tell who formed the first Canadian contingent of 30,000 men that went overseas? Will he tell me how many Ontario militia were in that force?

That is a mere side issue and does not disprove my argument. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) has claimed the credit for the militia of doing all these wonderful things. I maintain that if you take an equal number of men from our farms and factories who have the right spirit and enthusiasm they are the equals in performance of the organized militia. When I spoke upon these estimates last year I endeavoured to point out that the money we were asked to vote was not for the maintenance of a defence department for Canada. I tried to

show that the greater part, or at any rate a large part, of the money we were then asked to vote was being devoted to useless purposes. I also stated that in a good many instances, in my humble opinion, the money went to feed parasites. I expressed the opinion that the condition of agriculture in Canada, and the state of unemployment, was such that we ought not to be asked to maintain a military aristocracy, who were living on the fat of the land while the rest of our people were working too long hours and contributing heavily to the public treasury through taxation. It does seem to me that we should discuss here the general principle as to the desirability of such expenditure. As the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) has said, it is at the commencement of a new parliament that we should come to a distinct understanding as to whether we are going to continue military expenditure upon the scale on which it has been maintained in the past. I desire to ask who is the common enemy who threatens us? Why do we want a defence force in this country? These are questions which should be discussed at this time, and if the will of Parliament is that the voting of such moneys should continue we will submit to that decision. Otherwise, such large appropriations should not be continued to be asked for these purposes. It seems to me that a little Peace Conference should be called in Ottawa at this time to decide upon the policy we should follow in the future. Throughout the world different countries are calling for a stop to military expenditures nevertheless in Canada there are individuals clamouring that it be maintained, and trying to imbue the people with the idea that there is a common enemy to be feared and met. My hon. friend from North Toronto, of course, likes to have large military expenditures in the city from which he comes. But when he speaks for North Toronto and takes this attitude I have a right to speak for Assiniboia, a purely agricultural constituency, and take a contrary stand. I think I am right in saying that the greater part of the revenue which this Government receives from the province of Saskatchewan comes from my own constituency, and what do we get in return for it? In former years the views of the agricultural people of Canada have not been adequately expressed here, but they now have a fair representation in Parliament, something they have not had before within the lifetime of this Dominion. The representatives of agriculture are here

S upply-M ili tia
now and they are going to stay, because they have a real mission to perform, and one of the aims of that mission is to see that this unwarranted expenditure is reduced.

I notice that a number of those who have spoken have criticised the expense of the militia on the ground that at the present time there is apparently no need of it. I would like to point out that when trouble arises, or when war breaks out, we do not receive notice. We do not get any such notice as that after a certain number of days a certain nation will proceed to war. That is not the way wars break out; as a rule they break out in the most unexpected manner. Who expected in June, 1914, that war would be declared in August following? I venture to say that no one in this Dominion made that prophecy. The militia of Canada is necessary up to a certain point in order that we may be ready for emergencies, because the most important point of all is that we do not receive notice of trouble. We may say that there is not likely to be any trouble to the south or to the north or anywhere else, or to be internal trouble; but these things arise with startling rapidity. It is the duty of every man in this country to protect his home and family, and, therefore, I say that the existence of the militia is necessary up to a certain point for the purpose of being prepared.
Another point to which I wish to refer is the training of men. There is, amongst members of the House, a great misapprehension in reference to trained men. Men were not taken off the farms nor from the towns and put into the front line without previous training. The men, who went to the front at the first and who were able to carry on until they were supplemented by others, were men who had already undertaken and undergone military training in this country. It was no time to put untrained men into the line, and a certain time for training is required. Apparently a number of members who have referred to this matter seem to think that men can be picked out and, in a short time sent to the front; but men required intensive training for about four months before they were put into the front line.
My other and last point is that the whole list of estimates, as submitted by the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham), appears to me to be a very reasonable and necessary amount. I have no doubt that, under the
new organization, this amount will give us efficiency; but I do not think it is desirable, wise, or safe to attempt to carry on the militia of this country with a smaller amount than that for which the Minister of Militia has asked.

I do not want to make any lengthy remarks; but there are a few words which might well be said to the committee, because, I am sure, no hon. member has any desire to misrepresent things as they exist. We are, I understand, considering only the first item of this appropriation, and in connection with that, remarks have been made which might lead the committee and the people generally to believe that unwarranted expenditure on gold lace is involved in these items. It is very easy to use the phrase " gold lace "; the words slip easily from every member's lips. They will, no doubt, be bandied about throughout the country, and they will succeed in adding to a prejudice which, unfortunately, exists in certain quarters towards the militia. Would hon. members be greatly surprised if I called their attention to the fact that, in the first item, not one pennyweight of gold lace is involved? Would they also be somewhat astonished if I told them-and if my assurance is not sufficient, it can easily be backed up by many hon. members in this House-that the officers of the militia of Canada pay for their own gold lace out of their own pockets, and they pay the customs duty upon it themselves? Let us deal with plain facts; let us not indulge in slurs and sneers against a large body of gentlemen who are contributing their time, brains and wealth towards keeping up the militia of Canada and who are getting not one dollar of return for so doing. That happens to be the fact; it may not be popular; it is not a good thing on which to make a stump speech; but it happens to be the fact, and, as regards the particular estimate under consideration, I will invite the careful attention of members to some of the items involved in it. One item is " care of arms." Hon. members will realize that, throughout this country, sometimes in armouries, but very often, in the rural districts, in the homes of commanding officers, rifles which have cost this country millions of dollars are placed, and they have to be taken care of by the officer commanding the unit who is responsible for those arms. The allowance for looking after those arms used to be $40.
Supply-Militia
Are those rifles that are being cared for Ross rifles, or some others?

I do not know anything about the Ross rifle. I am not talking about the Ross rifle; I am talking about the rifles that are the property of the Dominion of Canada and that are distributed in many places throughout Canada, the rifles which would be used if any active use should be required of rifles either inside or outside of this country by our militia.
There is equipment as well, as I am reminded, various clothing. There is not only the clothing, but there are the belts and other equipment; there are, in some places, guns, and these have all to be taken care of. In the days that I can speak of, I know the allowance to a rural commanding officer was $40 a year for looking after the rifles and equipment of his company or battery or whatever the unit happened to be. The allowance is a modest one; I do not think it has been increased, but the minister will correct me if I am wrong in so thinking. Where there is an armoury kept up out of the public funds, this allowance is not paid; but where the country saves the expense of a caretaker through some person undertaking to do this work in connection with his unit, he received the modest sum of $40, for this very valuable service. If this service was not performed, the rifles would be destroyed by rust, and millions of dollars of this country's investment would become nothing. That might possibly suit certain people in this country; but I do not think it suits the great majority of this Parliament, or the vast majority of the Canadian people.
The commanding officer is allowed $40 for postage which he has to spend, in rural districts especially, in communicating with members of his unit who live at considerable distances. He has to arrange, prior to annual training, to find out where his men are to see that they are got in, to see to the distribution of clothing to them, and to see that the clothing is returned after the season is over. If that service is not performed, that clothing is lost and millions of dollars are lost to this country. Therefore, hon. gentlemen who wish to reduce this item are really endeavouring to lessen the necessary services for taking care of the property of the country. One hon. member said-and I think he was candid-that he did not know how to attack these estimates in detail be-

cause he did not know what they stood for. I would suggest that the hon. member first search the Auditor General's report for the details in order that he may know what the items are, and then he will be in a position to criticise; but he should not rush blindly in and endeavour to strike out an appropriation which may mean the destruction, the loss to this country, of ten-fold, yes, a hundred-fold, of the amount involved in this appropriation.
Another item is "command pay" which is somewhat similar to what I have been explaining. The amount for drill instruction is received only when a man actually gives the time or some instruction in drill or hires someone else to do that work. I do not see how it is possible to maintain the services rendered under this item for one penny less than the amount involved. It is certainly no answer to talk about gold-lace which is worn by officers at their personal expense. If hon. members were keeping in touch with the militia, they would know that, since the war, gold lace has practically disappeared. There is no waste of money for ornament or show; the service is simply practically what a farmer does if he puts a house over his reaper or binder instead of exposing it to the weather, as, unfortunately, happens to be the case in some parts of the country with which I am fairly familiar. It is simply reserving a man's capital. If you want the capital of the country wasted, strike out an item like this and let millions of dollars go to pot.

My hon. friend (Mr. Baxter) has demonstrated what a great loss to the country it would be if we did not take care of old clothes and rifles at a cost of $120,000. Well, I think it might be advisable to burn these old clothes and destroy these rifles and save that $120,000. We shall have to spend $120,000 next year, and at that rate it would take only a few years to buy new rifles. An expenditure like this is only a waste of money. These estimates can be reduced by about $5,000,000, and I should like to know whether this is the time to bring in a resolution for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If such a thing were done there would be no militia force in the Dominion.

If it is proposed to reorganize the militia, it might facilitate and hasten that re-organization if the minister knew exactly how much money he had to

Supply-Militia
spend upon it. If we vote the full $11,000,000, or thereabouts, it is not likely that even he will hurry with the re-organization.
What was the approximate cost of the annual drill for the average year preceding the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If hon. members will allow the item now before the Chair to pass, I could better explain that question on the next vote.
Carried.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Annual Drill, $1,400,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These estimates are on the pre-war basis. Of course, the entire work of deflation has not, perhaps, yet taken place, but as the cost of everything approaches normal the expenses will be proportionally reduced. The drill in 1913, before there was any war at all, cost $1,800,000. The amount asked for this year, after the war, is really less than the pre-war vote, notwithstanding the fact that the dollar in 1913 was equal to approximately $1.75 now.
What was the financial condition of Canada prior to the war, and what is it now?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Undoubtedly it was better before the war, but in 1913 it was not too promising. At that time we were on the verge of hard times, as was indicated by several banking institutions in the world. That, however, is not the question. Do we need annual drill? That is the question.
What were the estimates in 1910, when there was a Liberal party in power with a good government?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The last I have are the estimates for 1910-11, but I may point out that, although brought down by the succeeding government, they were the estimates of their predecessors. The expenditure in 1910-11 was $7,067,000. That was practically equal to the estimate of to-day, if indeed it was not more, considering what the dollar could buy then as compared with now. Clothing for the troops now costs 50 per cent, 75 per cent and sometimes 100 per cent more, and so does maintenance. The salaries paid to all officers since the war have been higher because of the increase in cost of living, as recognized by every business man in the country. This year it is proposed to train half, or, at
most, 60 per cent, of the number of men trained in 1911. The purpose is merely to keep up what one hon. gentleman referred to as skeleton training, and'not full training at all. Full training, as my hon. friends who have been ministers will know, would cost three or four times more. I consulted with General MacBrien, the chief of staff, one of the best men in the Dominion in his position, a man who is careful financially and who made a wonderful record in the war. He is an honour to his calling, and he thinks it is necessary, if we are to have a militia in Canada, that we should keep up some training. If I were asking the committee to sanction a scheme of extensive training I should be open to criticism, but this does not provide for more than 60 per cent, or at most 65 per cent, training. I was criticised by a Toronto paper the other day for reducing the number of days from sixteen to nine. This vote provides for the training of 60 per cent of the force for nine days instead of sixteen, and the only criticism that I have heard so far is that the reduction has gone too far. I would leave it to hon. gentlemen who had sons, relatives and friends in the war. Are your boys, who have come back, looking to be trained? I do not think they are. But if any emergency arose and you needed men, do you think it would be fair for the men who went through hell for four years to be asked to undertake the same task again, without our calling upon the younger men to do some drilling to take their place? I do not expect that there will be war, but if we are to keep up a militia we must have some young men enter the militia every year. It is not fair to those who have gone through three or four years of war that we should stand aside and say we will not train others to take their places but will let them shoulder the burden as they shouldered it before.
Now, in discussing this matter with General MacBrien I took it up from every angle. I asked him what the effect would be on the militia if we had no training. There is a certain overhead expense we must keep up in connection with the officers and organization for the training that is given every year. General MacBrien gave it as his considered opinion that if we do not provide some training for our young men we will do an injustice to the militia that this House will hasten to rectify, perhaps in three or four years, at the expense five times as great as the sum I am asking for to-day. That being the case, I leave the decision to the House. I am strongly
Supply-Militia

in favour of having some training given each year to our young men. Our men who went overseas, God knows, had fighting enough. But those men have sons and brothers who are anxious to receive training and be ready to enter the permanent militia if required. If we expect to retain a militia force without that training, we may as well be prepared to abandon the service altogether.
Reference has been made to the permanent militia that did go overseas-and that did not go overseas, as one hon. member said. Let me point out that if it had not been for our trained officers you would never have got thirty thousand men across the ocean in the time you did. And many of the boys who were anxious to go were the sons of the men who had been in the permanent militia, the men who were trained in our militia camps-the camps we propose to hold this summer-were the men who were put in charge of our boys and trained them. As a result these boys were fit to go overseas in a few weeks; but without that training they would have had to remain here indefinitely and Canada would not have been able to achieve the proud position which she now occupies.
I am not a military officer, or a military man, but two of my boys trained as officers, and my experience was that an officer has to supplement his militia pay with a good deal of his private funds to keep up his company. The money we vote for training does not go into the pockets of the officers; they have to pay out hundreds of dollars of their own money to keep up their regiments. When it is charged that officers are living in luxury and having a lot of government money to put in their pockets, I know from my own experience that those officers spend a lot of their own money as well as all they get from the Government to keep the militia alive.

With regard to this item for annual training, I concur with what the hon. minister has said, particularly with the last part of his statement. The annual pay granted for the training of our militia does not go into the pockets of the officers, as some people seem to think. I am speaking particularly with regard to the training of what is known as a city corps. For years prior to the war I do not think any city corps that trained and drew its annual drill-pay ever put one cent of the money into the pockets of its officers, non-commissioned officers, or men; that money went back to maintain the efficiency of the corps which the gov-

eminent did not grant sufficient funds to keep up. Since the armistice the old militia units have been pretty well shot to pieces.
I take issue with some hon. gentlemen regarding the militia which did not serve overseas in the first instance. The first Canadian contingent mobilized at Valcar-tier was composed, to the extent of over 98 per cent, of officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the active militia. Now the active militia are endeavouring to get on their feet once more. This annual allowance for training is the only means by which these units can rehabilitate themselves. The foundation of the old city corps was kept together during the war period by those ex-officers and others who were too old to go overseas, hoping that when the war was over the old units would come into being again. That has taken place. The officers, non-commissioned officers and men of those respective units that served overseas have to the extent of pretty nearly 90 per cent gone back to their old units again, and those officers are bringing in the new generation of our young men to educate and train them in the work, but they are not getting one cent of pay for doing so. This annual drill-pay will be contributed back to the Government in the maintenance of those units that have been a credit to the country in the past, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) said, and I think they will continue to be a credit to Canada as long as Canada is a nation.
I think the vote should not be cut down one cent.
Increase it.

In fact, I should like to see it increased. As the minister goes along, he may not require the whole amount. I know last year a small percentage was spent in training simply because the ranks were not filled up rapidly; but large numbers of the units to-day, as I know personally, are up to their old peace establishment of 1913. All the more credit to them. They are not getting any pay out of it. The item of command pay is in the same category. A small allowance was given to officers commanding corps for command pay, but I do not believe that any officer in our militia ever put a cent of that money in his pocket. We have heard talk about gold lace. I would point out that any equipment officers had was paid for out of their own pockets and never a cent was contributed out of the money voted by Parliament.

Supply-Militia

I have listened with a great deal of surprise to what has been said this afternoon respecting the militia of this country. The hon. member for Prince Edward Island comes nearest to my view in his remarks. I am always astonished when I contrast the attitude of a minister putting his estimates through with his attitude when he sat on the other side of the Chair. When we are on the Opposition side we have not the same views regarding expenditure. I remember very well that last year the Prime Minister of to-day found the militia vote too heavy and moved to cut it down by fifty per cent. I was pleased to support him. Now I am surprised to-day that one of his ministers should, in the first session of this new Parliament, ask for practically the same amount of money to be spent for militia purposes as was required last year. As we all know, our national revenue has in the meantime fallen off very materially. But notwithstanding that, it is now proposed to spend the same amount of money on the militia as was spent last year, although we were supposed to have been engaged in a war to end war. Not only so, but quite recently we sent representatives to the Disarmament Conference in Washington. Is it any wonder that the farmers of this country are tired of the schemes of politicians here in Ottawa to spend money for nothing?
The Minister of Militia said a few moments ago that we are spending very much more money to-day because everything is dearer. We are not surprised to learn that the pay of the militia is higher than it was in 1910 and 1911. But we farmers have also to pay more for our men than we did before the war. What do we do to meet this? We simply reduce the number of our employees. I can speak from personal experience in regard to this, because before the war I used to hire four men all the year around for my farm work at a total cost of $1200; but now that I have to pay $500 or $600 to each man I have to get along with two assistants; I cannot afford more. Now, if that is the condition with the farmer, it is equally the condition with this Government. Things have changed since 1919. We have spent, I understand, over two billion dollars, for what purpose? "To win the war" as we say in this House. Our financial condition is bad and will be for a century to come, I suppose; will any hon. member say this afternoon that we are to raise more soldiers to go into another European war? For myself, I say no. The people of my county
will not be satisfied with any suggestion made by hon. members of the Opposition in this House that the militia estimates are too low. I do not like that kind of business. I do not like to receive compliments from my opponents or to have them suggest that we are not spending enough money for militia purposes. I rather think that we are spending too much, and that is what I used to say when I sat on the Opposition side. Now that I am sitting on the Government benches I have not changed my view, nor will I do so.
One of my colleagues declared ..his afternoon that we should not cut out the entire amount of the vote for training the young men because we have experts at the present time in the Militia Department, and we must use those experts. In reply, I may say this: I want to keep the experts, and if they are not busy during the coming spring and summer, why should they not do some training among themselves-the colonels, the majors and the generals of all kinds? And. when they are tired of that training I invite them to spend a few weeks on a farm and work during haying time and harvest time. That would be great training for them.
I do not know what force would actually be required to keep peace in our territory. But our people are all good people, and I think a force of eighteen hundred men would be sufficient for the whole country. The rest of the men can be sent to the east or to the west, wherever they are needed on the farms. The farmers will pay them, so that the country will not be obliged to meet that expense, and the result will be a benefit to the country as a whole.

In the beginning of his remarks the hon. member stated that another hon. member shared his views, and he referred to him as the member from Prince Edward Island. I think he meant the member for Hants (Mr. Martell), did he not?

No, I referred to the member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes), who said that we were spending too much money on the militia and that we should arrange to have a force no larger than necessary to keep peace within the country.
Now, when we did have a great militia force the country could afford to pay for it. In 1912 and 1913, and in the first part of 1914, the government of the day were preparing for war and we had war. Now the war is over; we have no money to spare for anything that is not necessary, and I
Supply-Militia

therefore intend to move that this item of $1,400,000, in its entirety, be cut out of the estimates for this year. Let us sign an armistice for two or three years under which we shall stop spending .[DOT] money for nothing, and if the time comes when we have need of soldiers, we will find a way, as we did in 1914, to get the men we need.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the minister (Mr. Graham) on this item. As he spoke I recalled what took place in this House last session and the session before, when a similar item was under discussion. I could not help wishing that I had had the present minister's assistance on those occasions when I was trying to explain, in my humble way, why this vote of a million and a half for annual drill should be granted. I took the ground, it so happens, that he has taken to-day. I pointed out that the threlf or four hundred thousand men who had fought for three or four years in France or Flanders were, perhaps, the most finished soldiers in the world. They certainly required no more training; besides they had done their bit, if any men in this country or any men in the world had ever done their bit, and should not be asked for further services. I tried to show the House that it was advisable to bring on a new crop of trained men, and that for that purpose this money was necessary. But on both occasions hon. members now sitting opposite did not take that view of the situation. In the session before last the leader of the Opposition himself, now Prime Minister, moved to reduce this item by between eleven and twelve hundred thousand dollars, to leave, I think $300,000 odd as the amount for annual drill. And listen to his argument on that occasion. The present Prime Minister stated, page 3675 Hansard of 1920:
X would ipoint out that we have in this country at the present time an army of experienced men who need no drilling, men who have been through the war and have suffered its hardships. No amount of drilling in the world will make them more efficient than they are to-day, and until we are through with the work of demobilization we can well afford to dispense altogether with annual drills.
In other words, we should ask the very men whom the minister pictured in such glowing terms a moment ago-we should ask these heroes of the war to do the work that younger men should do. We should call upon them to defend the country in order that the present crop of young men that is growing up should be exempted.

The House, I am glad to say, negatived the motion of my hon. friend the Prime Minister. It was his view then that this item should 'be reduced by between eleven and twelve hundred thousand dollars, and he so moved. But now he is Prime Minister; he is head of the Government that comes in with the same vote, reduced by $100,000, and there is no explanation from him of the changed situation. Last session in this House the then member for West Kent, Mr. McCoig, now a senator, who always prided himself on being a farmer member, moved that the vote be reduced by $750,-000-a pretty substantial reduction. Every member of the Opposition, now sitting on the Government side, who was in the House just eleven months ago, voted for that reduction. They are there to-day, ranged behind the Prime Minister and his friends, supporting practically the same vote they condemned twelve months ago. Into the House at the present moment steps my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) . He took the same view a year ago. I have before me his statement on that occasion. He said:
But, I do humbly submit this is not the time for these things. My hon. friend the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), himself a gallant returned soldier, the other day reminded us of an important fact. We have 400,000 trained soldiers in Canada to-day-the best material for fighting that the world has ever produced. These men can be called upon if any emergency arises.
That is pretty definite. He goes on:
Why we should anticipate any emergency at this time it is not easy for anybody to conjecture. If there ever was a time when we had need of tout little military expenditure it is to-day, and I believe the men who will be most ready to confirm that view will be the returned soldiers themselves.
That is all the difference between promise and performance. They sat in opposition a year ago and condemned the proposed expenditure. They voted loudly for its reduction and they gave the reasons I have just quoted to the House. And so for the last two sessions. What, then, must they think to-day of the Minister of Militia in their own Government who proposes practically the same vote, with just as good reasons, the same reasons as were given to the House last year and the year before, the same solid, substantial reasons, because I maintain the vote should be granted, and granted without hesitation. But what shall we say of the sincerity, of the honesty, of men who on two occasions during the last two sessions have deliberately voted to reduce? Do you wonder

Supply-Militia
that some of their own followers have been misled? Do you wonder that my hon. friend who last spoke in the committee is a little disappointed? Do you not believe that he had reason for thinking when he came to the House this session that there would be something substantial by way of reduction? I am glad there is not. I am glad they have in the new minister a man who sees the necessities of the situation, and a man strong enough to maintain what is the proper stand in connection with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I wish to
point out to my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Guthrie) that there is something very different in the situation as it presents itself to the House this year, and as it presented itself two years ago and last session. May I remind my hon. friend that two years ago when we took exception to this vote, his government had in the estimates a vote running into several millions of dollars, I think, for the purpose of demobilization. We in opposition at that time took the position that until demobilization had been completed, until the Government had got through spending millions of dollars on demobilization, there was no justification for putting in these large amounts for the purposes of annual drill.

Have you not got that
vote this year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, we have not. We may have some claims, but not for the purpose of demobilizing the men from overseas.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is just christened
under another name.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not at all.
At the time I speak of, the Government were still bringing men under arms from across the sea. There is nothing of that kind in the estimates at this time. There is a great difference. When exception was taken by those of us in opposition at that time to the expenditure on account of annual drill, it was because the Government was asking us at the same time to vote millions of dollars for the purpose of demobilizing men who had been serving actively. We contended that as long as we were paying out money for demobilization purposes, we should not be asked to pay further large sums for annual drill. That is a very different situation from the one that presents itself at the present time, when demobilization has been completed,
and we have to decide whether we shall continue to have a militia in this country or abandon it altogether.

I cannot allow my hon. friend to get away with that statement, because it is not correct. He says that at the time we were bringing men home from overseas. I will challenge him to prove that statement. Demobilization at that time was completed, and the hon. gentleman who sits beside me (Mr. Mewburn) retired as Minister of Militia in 1919. Between 300 and 400 men were kept in Great Britain packing up material to be shipped to this country. These men were demobilized in the autumn of 1921. There may have been 200 or 300 men in Europe in the session the year before last, the session of 1920, engaged in packing up, but last session when the vote was made to reduce there was none. We were not bringing men home. The vote called the demobilization vote was not in the estimates for that purpose but it was for the purpose of paying war claims that had not then [DOT]been adjusted and paid, transportation claims largely, claims with the British Government, and claims of shipping companies. Between $30,000,000 and $40,000,000 was in the estimates for that year and last year between $6,000,000 and $7,000,000 was there for the same purpose. This year the Government has changed the wording of the vote. Instead of calling it demobilization they have called it "Adjustment of War Claims." It appears on page 71 of the estimates, and amounts to $8,411,800. If my hon. friend says he moved to reduce this vote in 1920 because there was a demobilization vote, I tell him that he has one there in the estimates now under a different name. If the motion to reduce was made last year because we had between $6,000,000 and $7,000,000 for demobilization, I tell him that he has a larger one still in the estimates under a different name.
Why not let us have a candid statement? They were in opposition in those days and they were pandering for what they supposed was popular support; they were pandering in this House, without thinking the matter out as they should have done, for popular support, and they boldly proposed on both occasions to cut this vote down to the vanishing point, where it would have been absolutely worthless as a vote for that purpose, and on each occasion the Government had to muster its followers and vote the motion down. Twelve months have gone and they are now in power and
Supply-Militia

in a position to carry out their ideas. Do you think they intend to do it? Is it any wonder that my hon. friend down there feels disappointed that he has been fooled in the matter?
There is nobody to fool me in this House.

I do not believe anybody in this House can fool him, but he had reason to expect at all events that these deliberate actions of the Opposition only twenty-four months ago would be put in practice at the first session of Parliament. I am glad they were not put in practice. All I want to do now is to show the hollowness of the contention of the Opposition in former years, and particularly in view of what the Government proposes to do at the present moment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If what my hon. friend says is correct, then he deceived the House in the matter of demobilization, as he did in the matter of the purchase of ammunition. He told this House in regard to ammunition for artillery purposes that there was need for a very large vote running into a hundred thousand dollars or thereabouts, because the ammunition for artillery purposes had to be manufactured in our Canadian arsenals. We found out afterwards that my hon. friend was bringing in from the Old Country ammunition, high explosive shells, amounting it is estimated to $6,000,000, out of a credit which was to this country's account in the Old World. He has still to account to Parliament for that expenditure, and I will expect before this debate is over that he will do so. If what he says is true about demobilization, he deceived us in the same way in that regard, for he distinctly led us to believe that the reason why we had to vote this large sum for demobilization was because men were still overseas and had to be brought back, and our contention was, if that were true there was no necessity for voting money for annual drill in Canada.

I assume that my
hon. friend will verify his statement. What I said will be in Hansard and I assume that my hon. friend will produce it. I am going to deal with the ammunition question, but as it is six o'clock it would be hardly worth while starting on it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might be explosive.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the Chair and the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
