speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
explain what this means?

I will be very glad to explain. This is Bill No. 6 "An act respecting the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway Company". The railway in question is a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The bill grants that company authority to build a railway or rather, I should say, renews the authority for them to build this extension of a railway in Vancouver Island from a place called Courtenay to Duncan Bay, a distance of thirty-six miles, in the district that I represent. The bill extends for five years the period in which the company can build this railway which is only to be thirty-six miles long. The bill itself says the company may begin construction in two years and complete the road within five years; but as a matter of fact it really gives them five years to begin and end the construction of the railway because the company do not come, in that regard, under the ordinary provisions of the Railway Act of Canada which requires the expenditure of fifteen per cent of the value of the line within two years upon construction. That provision does not apply to the present bill, it is overridden by a special clause, so that the company really get five years in which to begin to build the railway. Now my amendment will reduce the period in which the company must begin construction to one year, and the period within which it must complete the line to three years. I wish to disavow any spirit of hostility to the Canadian Pacific Railway

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Railway
Company in any way whatsoever. I believe they are a great and very well managed company and I would be very glad to see them running our National railways. But that has nothing to do with this situation. If the company are as anxious to build this railway as they say they are-and my constituents are equally anxious-then we are all united on the subject. In that case we want to do the Aaron and Joshua act and hold up the hands of this railway Moses who seems somewhat inclined to let the tide of railway construction, the tide of battle, go against him as in the case of Moses of old.
I can give three reasons why this railway should be built at once:	In the first
place the company have had five years to build it and have not done so. But apart from that, the construction of the railway would provide a great deal of very necessary work. We hear much in this House about unemployment and we hear of hundreds of thousands of dollars spent in alleviating unemployment, very largely in non-productive work the greater portion of which is a loss. Then too, there could be no more opportune time than the present to build this railway bearing in mind the question of labour. Labour is probably as cheap now as it will ever be, unless the cost of living takes a very great change of which there is no immediate prospect. In addition to that, if this enterprise were proceeded with, it would give a very great amount of very much needed work for the people in that vicinity and relieve the labour situation on Vancouver Island and in Vancouver city. As you know there is a great deal of unemployment in Vancouver at the present moment. In the second place access would be given to a great number of people who have been living there hoping, and praying and expecting this railway for something like fifty-five years. Comox Valley is one of the oldest settled districts in British Columbia. It is a very fine, fertile valley, and these people went in there many years ago with "the sure and certain hope," as the Church of England Prayer Book says, of the railway coming along, and they are living in that hope to-day. Not only that, Sir, but it would lay open to settlement large areas of fine agricultural land. These areas would be made easy of access and would be most suitable places for settlement by some of that herd of immigrants we are told it is the policy of the Government-they have a vote of something like $400,000 in the estimates for the purpose-to bring into the country. We
are told these immigrants are coming along, and the Government could not get a more splendid or more fertile valley in which to locate them-if they are going to get them- than in the same Comox Valley. As I say this railway would give access to those lands.
I have cited the arguments in favour of having this railway built. Now, as to possible arguments against it. I am handicapped in that regard because I cannot think of any such arguments, and having to speak first in this discussion it is hard for me to anticipate any possible opposition. The only way in which I could anticipate any opposition is to revert back to the statements made to the Railway Committee when this matter was under discussion there. I may say in passing, Sir, that the transactions in the Railway Committee revealed to me, as a new member of the House, a somewhat remarkable condition of affairs. It appears that, according to the rules, and the dictum of a gentleman named Bourinot-who I understand is an authority and has been dead for some time-when a railway bill of this character comes before the Railway Committee there is allowed to appear before that committee and argue the merits of the case the learned counsel of the law employed by the railway in that behalf. That occurred in this case and I have no objection whatever to the appearance of the counsel in question; he did not abuse his opportunities in any way whatever. I merely state that he was allowed to present his case as fully and as often as he thought necessary. But when it came to the member who represents the district through which this railway is to run, on account of his not being a member of the committee he was not allowed to represent the views of that district at all. As a matter of fact I was able to make some observations concerning the bill because it was not known at that time that I was not a member of the Railway Committee. When it was discovered that I was not a member of the committee, owing to my honesty in not voting when a vote was taken, immediate objection was raised to my activities, and had it not been that Providence-ever kind to the under-dog- sent to my assistance an angel disguised- perhaps I should say thinly disguised-in the fleshly form of the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell), I would not have been able to get my amendment before the committee at all. At any rate there is the condition of the rules. It may be

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Railway
argued-I have heard hon. members assert that I have exaggerated the case-that even though an hon. gentleman is not a member of the committee he is allowed to go there and speak his mind provided he does not vote. As to that, let me say that the question was brought up in the Committee on Agriculture a few days ago and it was decided-absolutely decided on the authority of the gentleman I mentioned a moment ago, Bourinot (page 469) -
"That a member of the House who is not a member of the committee has no right whatever to attend such committee for the purpose of addressing it, or putting questions to the witnesses, or interfering in any way with the pr oceedings."
If that is one of the rules which I and other new members are supposed to receive with reverence, to handle with loving care and to hand on, unimpaired, to our successors, then I would suggest that the sooner we have a bonfire of those rules the better, and let us start out with a fresh set of rules more in accord with those that would be common and customary in an ordinary commercial or industrial undertaking. Let us get a little more down to business and have a little less of these rules. As I have said before, I understand the author is dead, so he will not feel hurt at any criticism, but I think he should have taken some of those rules with him.
I now propose to deal with the arguments advanced before the committee. I think, however, "argument" is an ill-advised word, for argument suggests, does it not, a basis of fact and a superstructure of logic? I could not help thinking, when I heard the statements made in that regard, that both the logic and the facts were somewhat wobbly. I will not call them arguments; I will call them statements made in that connection. The first one was that this was part of a big railway, a main railway I think was the expression used, from Victoria at the south end of the island to the north end of the island; that 140 miles had been built, and there was a general impression given that there was a vigorous and aggressive building movement going on and that, whenever they had a moment to spare, they turned and dug a few more miles of this railway. It is true that the railway runs from Victoria; but it does not run to the north end of the island, and the company has not a charter to do that. It stops at Duncan's Bay. The railway has been built from Victoria to Courtenay, 140 miles having been built

recently, we were given to understand. Of this 140 miles, 75 miles were built under the terms of the union of British Columbia with the confederation. That takes us back a good many years, and it was built, not by the Canadian Pacific, but by a gentleman by the name of Dunsmuir who received, for the building of those 75 miles of railway, a large sum, I forget the exact figure, but practically enough to build the road, and he also received a grant of practically one-third of Vancouver island. This grant took in everything, base metals and coal mines as well. One of the members for Vancouver the other night, in speaking of the natural resources of British Columbia, mentioned this land grant to the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway, and he said that it was conservatively estimated as being worth $25,000,000. When one considers that there are six or eight very valuable coal mines on the island and a vast quantity of timber and base metals, perhaps he was right; but at any rate, enough money to build the railway and $25,000,000 worth of land were paid to build 75 miles of this railway thirty-eight years ago. Therefore, I do not think it enters very much into the consideration of whether this franchise should be extended to-day or not. Twenty-eight years later, they took another burst of railway construction and they built another sixty-five miles. That was some twelve years ago; and if we are going on the same geometrical progression of railway construction, the cycle when another burst of railway construction to complete this thing will come around will, so far as I can figure it, be the year 1948. I am wrong-1946 was the correct date. About that time I fear-I will not fear, but I trust many of those men, including myself, who have waited so long and faithfully for that railway, will be in a happier country where railways will not be needed and where politicians are excluded also. In that happier clime I would hate to meet my constituents and hear them say to me: "You did not get that railway built." Another statement that was alleged as a reason why this extension should be granted and against my proposal to shorten the period in which it would be built, was that there was a lack of funds. Lack of funds for the Canadian Pacific to build thirty-six miles of a railway in a comparatively level country! A bait was thrown out to the Progressive members who were present. It was suggested that it would not be fair to the rest of Canada for the

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Railway
Canadian Pacific to concentrate all their building energies on this 36 miles of railway on Vancouver island. But I think the Progressive members and other members who were present have sufficient acumen to understand that their opportunities of getting railways will not be impaired, even if the Canadian Pacific are compelled to spend their vast resources in building 36 miles of a railway on Vancouver island, the work being spread over three years. I may mention that it is supposed-I would not guarantee this-that the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway is one of the most profitable extensions of the whole Canadian Pacific. I do not believe the Canadian Pacific, that great company with its high standing and reputation, would approve its apologists who say that it would impair its credit or finances if it built that railroad in three years instead of five. About 30 miles from this identical place, I travelled over a logging railroad 40 miles in extent, and as well built and ballasted as the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway is, and that railway was built by that logging company without any subsidy from this House and without any fuss being made about the matter. I saw that road built simply to get out logs, and there are many reasons why it would be more advantageous to build this particular road.
Another statement that was made as a reason why they should be given practically unlimited time was-I will prove later on, that this is only a precursor of more similar bills, for there is no intention of building under this bill-" you might as well give it to them for if you do not, no one else will build the railway." There may be a certain amount of cynical truth in that statement, because, if there was any prospect of opposition, this railway would have been built long ago. We will consider that point later. The one thing that I am certain of is that no other railway company is likely to come here asking for a charter as long as the great Canadian Pacific has a blanket charter to build this line.
There is one of the best water powers in British Columbia along the line of this railway, and I am told that negotiations are going on to-day by a large English syndicate to harness that power. For that purpose they would require to have a capital of between three and four million dollars. Suppose I come here next year on account of the Hydro-Electric Company asking for a charter, what a howl would go up. I would be a destructionist, a financial Bolshevist and everything else: I would be interfering with vested interests, and I would be howled down. But why not give these people an opportunity?
Apart from that, there is another aspect to which I should like to draw the attention of the House. Some years ago, when the railway boom was prevalent and everybody was building railways, the Canadian Northern, now the National railways, got a charter on the Island to build from Victoria up to Courtenay, the place I am now talking about. They spent $3,000,000 and they got the railway graded, but no steel on it, as far as six miles from the west coast at Port Alberni. Since then they have laid steel to Cowichan lake to get out some valuable timber there. That has been done by the government; it shows that they have it in contemplation, and there is no reason to suppose that they will let the $3,000,000 which they have already spent there, lie idle. It may be in time to come they will extend it, and if they do extend it, the line will run from Victoria to Courtenay and from there north. We were told in 1896 that a vast industrial boom took place on account of the accession of the Liberal party to power. It may be- I do not know-that history will reproduce itself and we shall see another industrial boom. If that is the case, it may well be that, in the course of a few years, the Canadian National Railways may find it possible to continue the railway further north. Amongst other industries that I might mention that would be touched by that line is the anticipated radium mine of British Columbia. I am proud of it. I do not believe there is another spot on the North American continent where radium has been found except in the district I have the honour to represent. Now, radium is not found like placer gold nor is it as easily gathered and put into a suitcase; it is found in rocks and involves an expensive process of handling. It is found within ten or twenty miles of the line of this railway; and this Is the day, and British Columbia the place, of unexpected development. We never know the moment some big company may take hold of it, and it might well be that if this railway is not built under this charter some other corporation might be found to build it. The most fatal objection that was raised was the one on which the lawyers and politicians are alike agreed: it was the fatal one of precedent. We find, Sir, that precedent haunts the very precincts1 of this House. It was stated that we had in the

Esquimau-Nanaimo Railway
dim past established the precedent that two years to commence and five years to finish was the ordinary rule with regard to railways, and: that because we had once laid down that rule, therefore we must forever adhere to it. Now, it would be all very well if this were a big railway, or even if this were the first time that these people were asking for this concession. But this is the second reincarnation of this railway, and it does not necessarily follow that they should have the same time in which to build and finish. They know now what they are up against and have had ample time for preparation; and if an extension is granted now they will come back two years hence, asking another extension. In any case, this custom that is spoken of with such awe and respect has been in force only for a few years; and are we never to learn from experience that if certain legislation or certain regulations do not produce the object aimed at, we should abandon hoary-headed precedent and strike out for ourselves? Are we never to take a chance? Perhaps hon. members of the Government would not be sitting where they now are if the electors, on December 6th last, had not decided to take a chance ; and I think that the chance taken by the electorate was quite as great as the chance we should take in getting away from precedent now. It is yet in the womb of time whether the wisdom of the country was justified in her children on that occasion; but, I think, the chance the people took on that occasion was, if anything, much more desperate than the one I am asking the House to take to-night in abandoning precedent for once.
There is something else I want to point out. It has been the custom of this House always to defer to the findings of the Railway Committee. Word will go around that the railway committee has investigated the subject, and we must stand by their decision. At the bottom of members' minds is the idea: "It will save us the trouble of making up our minds for ourselves if we accept the findings of the committee." Well, may I remind the House of the precedent which we established quite recently? Only a few days ago there was introduced into this House a report of the Agricultural Committee in connection with the Wheat Board. That report had been unanimously arrived at in the committee; yet,, when it was brought into the House it was torn to pieces, the House unanimously deciding to send it back whence it had come. But this legis-

lation, which I am asking to have returned to the Railway Committee, was carried only by a narrow majority in a comparatively small meeting of the committee. I think, therefore, that we have ample reason for not adhering to the principle that because the Railway Committee passed on the question we must necessarily be prohibited from exercising our own judgment as well.
There is something else about the bill which more than ever convinces me that it is not intended to build under this charter, but to continue for another series of years the present state of things. We are all aware, Mr. Speaker, of the custom in connection with all these bills-and I have another one, No. 5, before me now- to insert a clause specifying the amount of bonds that are allowed to be issued against each mile of railway to be built. That clause was in the original act relating to this railway; but is it in this bill? It is not. They did not think it worth while putting it in. And they have either forgotten, omitted or neglected to put in even the customary clause giving the wretched bill a name. Are they so ashamed of this poor foundling that they have disdained to give it a title in the ordinary way? And when we find the omission of another clause with regard to the spending of 15 per cent in the two years, we are more than ever driven to the conclusion that they regard the whole thing as a stop-gap and have no intention of building under it. If they did intend to build, would they not have put in the clause about the bonds for the money to be provided to build with and would they not have given the poor foundling a name? They will be coming back two years from now and two years thereafter; and will simply regard this as a blanket charter from year to year and from decade to decade. This is unfair and unbusinesslike. It is unfair to the men who are living in that district, the pioneers who are expecting a railway; it is unfair to the men of the past, and unfair to the men of the future; for some hon. members may not realize that immigrants coming from the old country are very often misled by legislation of this character. Real estate men who have farms and lands to sell will show those immigrants this bill and say: " Look at that! There, under the imprimatur of the Government of Canada, is the assurance of a railway." And the poor deluded immigrant, unfamiliar with our system of doing business, will think this railway will be built. I have known

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Ry.
cases where men have gone in and built a home ahead of the railway on the strength of such a promise and the railway was not built for twenty-five years. It is not fair to the people who are already there, nor to those who may come hereafter, and I am not asking for anything unreasonable. I simply want a fair and just compromise. I am not saying that we should compel them to live up to the old charter, in which case they would have to begin operations immediately; I am merely asking that they shall begin operations within one year and complete within three years.

I have listened with considerable interest to the remarks that have been made with regard to the construction of this railway. I am familiar with the conditions prevailing on Vancouver Island and particularly with the proposed route of the railway in question. The Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway is asking for an extension of the line from the present terminus at Courtenay to a point at or near Duncan Bay, a distance of some thirty-six miles. This is not through country that is not fairly well supplied, at some reasonable distance, with water communication; it is located on an island, and there are fair roads through a good part of that country. The case of the railway company was presented to the committee and thoroughly threshed out, and it received the approval of the committee. Conditions have not yet reached normal, and we know that certain expenses are high in connection with railway construction, although prices have a downward tendency; and it is only fair to grant the reasonable request made by this railway-not an unusual request either-for an extension of time in order to complete the road. There is no other railway in that section of Vancouver Island this proposed line could couple up with except the railway now in operation and having its terminus at Courtenay. I do not think there is much danger about settlers being deceived. A settler should know enough to keep his eyes open when coming to Canada, and he should be very diligent in protecting his own interests. Anybody can tell a settler that a railway is to be built in some place or other. It is the settler's business to protect himself by securing proper information. I trust the House will accept the finding of the Railway Committee and grant the extension of time.

The question involved in this discussion has already been fully threshed out before the Railway Committee. That it was not possible for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, or any other company, to build the railway is quite evident by the fact that nothing was done under the charter, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company now comes before Parliament for an extension of time. If no extension is granted, it is pretty certain that no other company will build this railway. Even if the extension is granted, it will be fully six or seven months before the promoters are ready to begin work in the field, because financial arrangements will have to be made and extensive engineering plans prepared. So it is not likely that within the twelve months' extension which my hon. friend (Mr. Neill) proposes the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will be able to commence operations. As a matter of fact they are asking for an extension oi two years. Neither before the committee nor before this House, has it been proven that any other company intend to undertake this work if the Canadian Pacific Railway Company default. If another company were ready to proceed, provided this charter were not renewed, then there might be some ground for refusing the request of the promoters; but in the absence of any such competitors I think the full extension of two years should be granted. Obviously, an extension of only one year would not be sufficient to enable the Canadian Pacific railway to complete construction and it would only necessitate their coming back and asking for a further extension next session. We are asking therefore that the time be extended for two years.
If the hon. member will permit me? When he says "We are asking for an extension" whom does the "we" refer to?

I mean the members who advocate the granting of the promoters' request. I am not surprised at my hon. friend's question. The remarks of those of his friends who were opposing the bill before the Railway Committee almost led to a row on that very same point. The as. person that the hon. gentleman is trying to cast upon us is weak indeed. I think, Mr. Speaker, that we should not curtail the extension of time which the petitioners have asked for, but should give them such further time as will allow them to commence the work and carry it to completion. If



Esquimalt-Nanaimo Ry.
they do not begin construction within the specified time, then my hon. friend's argument can be advanced should the petitioners come back for a further extension in future.

Mr. Speaker, I have much pleasure in supporting the motion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I think he has taken a very reasonable view of this proposition. The railway company have slept on their rights, so to speak, for a number of years; and whilst my hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) says that if another company could show that it intended to build this road it would be a good reason for not extending this charter, I submit, in all deference to his opinion, that having this charter upon the statute books is inferentially a prohibition against other people coming in and undertaking construction. If a company were incorporated for the purpose of building this road, when they put their stock upon the market they would at once be met by the assertion- and it would be an assertion of fact- that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company already held a charter for its construction.
We all know that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is	a large	and
powerful i corporation, so much so that when a member rises in the House to oppose it, he is to a great extent courting political oblivion.	But
when principle is involved it matters not to me whether it is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or any humble body of people associated for the purpose of building a railway, I think they are both entitled to equal consideration. So it is incumbent upon Parliament, I submit, to see that neither directly nor inferentially is an embargo placed upon any project to build a railway. As I have already stated, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, or its subsidiary, has had this charter for a number of years, and on divers occasions has come to this House for an extension of time. To-day a further extension is being sought without any legitimate reasons therefor being given.
The motion of my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni gives the petitioners an opportunity within the next twelve months to prove their 'bona fides. If they begin construction within the next eight or nine months, or even within the next eleven months, they will have amply demonstrated to Parliament and to the country that they are serious in regard to this matter, and I am sure they would have no trouble

in getting a further extension of their charter to complete the railway.
It is all very well to have railway charters upon our statute books, but I submit that it is in the best interests of the people that no charter be granted to any individual, firm or corporation for the construction of a public utility unless ample evidence be adduced to Parliament that the promoters are financially able to begin construction of the work for which authority is sought. Because, as I have already said, if we enact legislation for the construction of a public utility, it inferentially has the effect of debarring others from building that utility. It is time we called a halt to permitting a corporation or an individual, either the mighty Canadian Pacific or the humblest individual in Canada, to hold charters for the purpose of keeping other people from building railways in a particular section, or of building them when it suits their own convenience, not the convenience of the public at large. I am not a resident of British Columbia-
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "Hear, hear," but I assure him that I am a resident of a greater province-Nova Scotia. I am submitting to-night, however, the same arguments that I would submit were this a charter for a railway in my own province. What is the case of British Columbia to-day, as it has been so ably set forth by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) may be the case of Nova Scotia to-morrow; and Sir, in this age of democracy it is necessary that everything possible be done to retrieve the mistakes that have been made in the past, in order that we may at least retain for the people of the future the rights which are legitimately the rights of the people and not of any corporation.

Mr. Chairman, shortly before the committee rose at six o'clock, and while we were discussing this item of $1,400,000 for annual drill, I had taken occasion to comment upon the fact that last session a motion had been made in this House by the then hon. member for Kent county to reduce the amount then in the Estimates for annual drill by
9 p.m. one-half, and that the present Prime Minister of Canada and those now supporting him on the Government side had solidly voted in support of that reduction. I had likewise commented on the fact that in the year previous, in the session of 1920, my hon. friend the Prime Minister had himself moved in respect to this item, which then stood at the sum of $1,500,000, a motion that it he reduced by the sum of $1,150,000, to leave it the net amount of $350,000, and I made some comment on what I think I can reasonably call the change of front on the part of my hon. friend the Prime Minister in respect to this particular item. He moved the motion himself in this House in the year 1920.
This afternoon shortly before six o'clock he attempted to make a justification of his change of position. He attempted to justify his change of attitude, because to-day his Government has laid before the House a proposal to expend $1,400,000 for annual drill, by stating that in 1920 conditions were different, that we had then a large number of men practically under arms, undemobilized, and that that fact was present in his mind when he made the motion in 1920. I endeavoured, in reply, to point out to my hon. friend that he was entirely mistaken in that view, that we had very, very few men undemobilized when he made
Supply-Militia

his motion, that there were overseas only some 200 or 300 men who had not been returned to Canada. Then my hon. friend replied to me in language to which I think I may fairly take exception, or, at all events, I may ask him to justify the statement he made. He used this language:
If what my hon. friend says is correct, he deceived the House in the matter of demobilization as he did in the matter of the purchase of ammunition. If what he says about demobilization be correct, he deceived us in the same way in that regard, for he distinctly led us to believe that the reason why he had to vote this large sum for demobilization was because the men were overseas and had to be brought back and our contention was that if that were true there was no necessity for voting money for annual drill in Canada.
I do not know, Mr. Chairman, that I am what you would call over-sensitive in regard to language that is used in reference to myself, hut when the statement is made from his place in Parliament by the Prime Minister of this country that I have deceived the House in regard to the matter of demobilization, and that by reason of my deception my hon. friend then leading the Opposition made a motion to reduce the amount for annual drill in 1920, I think I may fairly ask him to justify his statement by telling the House just what I said in justification of the charge he has made against me. I have in the interval taken a look at Hansard, and I find that on the 16th of June, 1920, my hon. friend entered upon a fairly elaborate discussion of the militia estimates. I am going to quote from what he said (Hansard, page 3646):
But the point to which I wish particularly to direct attention is the minister's endeavour to draw a comparison between the expenditure on militia and defence at the present time and amounts that were voted prior to the war. The minister seems to think that at the present time we ought to vote an amount at least equal to amounts that were being voted prior to the war. That is where I take direct issue with him. Before the war it was pretty generally anticipated ; it was certainly said in official quarters that a menace was threatening the world, and that it was necessary to meet that menace by increasing our military and naval forces.
That argument was used as the ground for increasing military expenditures, and it was largely in anticipation of the danger of a great international disturbance that this country voted for military and naval purposes the sums of money which were appropriated at that time. But conditions are wholly different to-day. There is no world menace. Where does the minister expect invasion from?
May I ask the same question again tonight of my hon. friend?
The minister says that this expenditure is needed for the defence of Canada-defence against whom?

I ask my hon. friend the same question to-night.
There is no answer; there is no answer to be made. There is not an hon. gentleman on the other side who will say that a single nation at the present time has any hostile intention or attitude of hostility towards this country, or that there is the slightest danger of Canada being invaded from any quarter. Yet the minister asks us to-day to vote a sum that will bear comparison with expenditures voted on the eve of the terrible situation which occurred in 1914. I might further point out that prior to 1914, that, to be correct, during the period of the Liberal Administration, because the minister referred to that period, we had surpluses, not deficits in our public accounts, and we had a small national debt. To-day we have a colossal public debt; we have obligations that are wholly different, and we are not in the same position to begin to meet them. It is one thing to lay out sums of money on different appropriations when there are plenty of funds in the treasury, but it is quite another matter when the nation is trying to cope with an enormous deficit and to meet obligations such as the country heretofore has never been faced with, and when conditions are such that there is the strongest reason why we should economize in every possible particular, and especially in those particulars in which no satisfactory reason can be shown for large expenditures.
But the most important consideration of ail is this. The minister has spoken about the need for training camps, permanent barracks and the like. Prior to 1914, it was necessary to have men trained as soldiers; we had no trained men, or very few, but what is the position to-day? We have in this country to-day an army of trained men, the most efficient soldiers that will be found in any part of the world, so that the situation is wholly different from what it was prior to the war. The need for training to-day is not what it was prior to the war. We have the experience, knowledge, and attainments of thousands of men as our security and safeguard if there be need for such at the present time. That is a reason why, on this particular score, much could be done in the way of reducing expenditures.
I followed my hon. friend on the same date. I tried to give him full particulars, these are the particulars in which he charges I deceived the House. As reported at page 3676 of Hansard for the same day I stated, in reply to my hon. friend:
There are still undemobilized of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, of all ranks, 2,386 men out of a total enlistment of over 390,060. There is no other country which took part in the war that can show that result, or anything like it. Of these men 1,334 are employed in the depots in this country on military work; 632 are patients undergoing treatment in hospitals; 420 are on the medical and nursing staffs, orderlies and attendants in hospitals ; making a total of 2,386 undemobilized out of well nigh 600,000. In addition we have in England undemobilized 36 officers, 154 men and 63 members of the air force who have been transferred to the Canadian Expeditionary Force, or 253.
That, surely, Mr. Chairman, was a plain, direct unequivocal statement of the extent

to which demobilization had proceeded on that day in June when my hon. friend made his motion. Now, lest it be said that on the vote for demobilization, which is a separate vote, something was said by me, I have looked that reference up too, and I find that in reply to questions I said on the 30th June, as will be found at page 4552, that we had only between two and three hundred men undemobilized in Great Britain or overseas. I gave particulars that same day of the whole proposed expenditure of the Militia Department in connection with the thirty-eight millions for demobilization. This statement will be found at pages 4550 and 4551 item by item, showing what part of that vote was to be expended in Canada, showing likewise that $9,745,000 of it was to be expended by the Overseas Ministers in Great Britain- every detail, every particular as to money and as to men, and my hon. friend sat in his place and heard my statement. The statement made by my hon. friend in regard to me to-day is the statement which I have read to the House-namely, that my hon. friend based his motion for a reduction in 1920 upon the fact that I had deceived Parliament in connection with the demobilization vote, and that annual camps were not necessary in 1920 because large numbers of men were then coming from overseas to Canada and these were highly trained soldiers. I take exception to the language of the Prime Minister, very grave exception. If he made his statement recklessly, if he made it in a moment of heat, I suppose he can explain it. The Prime Minister has had to turn many pretty sharp corners this session. I have no doubt he had to lie awake at night sometimes to think up new excuses for his many changes of front. I do not mind what excuses he gives to the House for his latest change of heart; I do not know what has caused him to change his opinion in regard to annual drills-it matters not one whit to me. But I ask him if it is quite fair that he should seek to offer as an excuse for his change of opinion a baseless statement that somebody else has deceived the House of Commons? Did my hon. friend not take the same position last year just twelve months ago? Did I deceive him twice on the subject? I do not think I uttered a word in connection with the subject last year; if I did he will produce it to the House now. But I am dealing with the expenditure of 1920, and I have gone over the records and if there is anything else to be stated I trust my
hon. friend will give it to the House. Certain it is that so far as I am aware I gave the House in 1920 the fullest, the fairest, and the most exact statement of the situation as it then existed. The true reasons for the motion to reduce annual drill by $1,150,000 in 1920 which actuated my hon. friend were given by him to the House on that occasion when he admitted to the House and which I quoted a few moments ago.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when we speak of demobilization my understanding is that it is the reverse process of mobilization. When forces are being mobilized they are being brought out for a particular purpose; when they are being demobilized they are being disbanded for a particular purpose. I maintain that when the minister asked this Parliament to vote millions of dollars for the purpose of demobilization, the people of Canada and the members of this House understood by that term that the money was for the purpose of demobilizing the forces that had been mobilized, and if he was trying to get money for any other purpose he was deceiving the House. That is the position I took and I say it is a right and proper position. Now in regard to what I said this afternoon as to my hon. friend deceiving the House in the matter of shells, let me indicate to him just what I have in mind and-

Mr. Guthrie: As between the two arsenals I think Lindsaj? would be the better adapted, but there are military reasons for maintaining both arsenals. Mr. Lemieux: How many men are there at the Quebec arsenal?
Mr. Guthrie: At the present time, nearly 500. All our heavy ammunition and quick firing ammunition, as well as a large part of our rifle ammunition, is made at Quebec. Lindsay only manufactures at present small arms ammunition ; I do not think it has the equipment for making artillery ammunition.
Mr. Lemieux: I am informed that the munitions turned out by the Quebec arsenal were highly commended by military authorities during the war. Is that a fact?
Mr. Guthrie: I understand that our ammunition has been very highly commended, both that made at Quebec and that made at Lindsay. I doubt if any better ammunition is turned out anywhere.
I submit that, when my hon. friend told this House that all our heavy ammunition and quick-firing ammunition, as well as a large part of our rifle ammunition, were made at Quebec, he led every member of this House to believe that the appropriation, which he was asking Parliament to vote for purposes of ammunition, was necessary because we had to get that heavy ammunition from the arsenal at Quebec. That was in 1920. I now come to the Estimates of 1921, when my hon. friend was asking Parliament to appropriate money to pay for the salaries of inspectors of munitions. What did he say? At page 2782 of Hansard of April 29, 1921, I find this statement:
Mr. Guthrie: The inspector of ammunition at Quebec is Mr. Keightley. We have two arsenals, one at Quebec and one at Lindsay. From these arsenals a large amount of ammunition has been turned out, running into many millions, and in that connection it is necessary to have a competent inspector. No loss can be greater or more consequential than that resulting from defective ammunition. The item is reduced this year by 525,000 ; we have brought it down to the lowest .possible figure. There has been no attempt to disguise these items; they are carried now as they have been for fifteen or twenty years.
A little further down he made this statement:
Mr. Guthrie: This item covers arms and ammunition.
Mr. Power: Is this for small arms or for artillery stores?
Mr. Guthrie: About 200,000 rifles came back to Canada at the end of the war, and of these about 40,000 are at the present moment being overhauled. Many of these arms as returned were found to be more or less defective from wear, rough usage, or loss of some trifling detail affecting the serviceability of the whole arm. After these 40,000 are nepaired, they will be put back into stock. The amount of money involved in stores of arms and ammunition is very large; we have the stores on hand now, and they must be kept in shape and continually examined and inspected; otherwise, on

account of deterioration, heavy losses are liable to be incurred.
I submit that, when my hon. friend asked Parliament for the appropriation for that purpose, he clearly led the House to believe that all the ammunition that was required was in storage in this country at that time; that there were large quantities of it, and that, for that reason, he had to pay a large amount for salaries to inspectors of munitions, for whom he was asking a particular appropriation at that time. I ask the committee to keep together in mind these two statements-the statement on June 17, 1920:
All our heavy ammunition and quick-firing ammunition, as well as a large part of our rifle ammunition, is made at Quebec.
And the statement of April 29, 1921:
The amount of money involved in stores of arms and ammunition is very large; we have the stores on hand now, and they must be kept in shape and continually examined.
Those statements, in the absence of any other reference to munitions available from any other source, I contend, imply and can only imply that we were getting all our munitions in this country and that, for that reason, Parliament should vote the amounts that were asked for. The committee should note what the Minister of Militia and Defence of that day said, which is in the paragraph preceding the one about munitions :
About 200,000 rifles came back to Canada at the end of the war, and of these about 40,000 are at the present moment being overhauled.
He spoke about arms coming back from the other side. Nothing was said about munitions. He made it perfectly plain, or rather he tried to convey the impression that all our munitions were manufactured in the arsenal at Quebec. Elsewhere in the debate, I think it will be found that he defended the fact of the amount asked for being so large by stating that it was because wages had gone up at the arsenals where these munitions were being produced. It was in the light of that discussion, of those statements, that this House appropriated money for munitions, for high explosives for the artillery. What do we find? I have in my hand a memorandum of gun ammunition entered at the outport of Levis, Que. I will not go any further back than May of last year. Remember it was in April of last year that my hon. friend's statement was made to the effect that we had all the stores here, and that he got the appropriation for the purpose of munitions. Why did he not, when he was asking this House to vote money for high explosive shells, say that we had a right, if we had it, to bring from the Old Country, out of some credit to which we were entitled there, munitions to the extent of $2,879,468 ? He said not a word about that; nor would the country have known anything of it, if it had not been that, passing the port of Levis one day, I saw one of these Government merchant marine ships laden with high explosive shells, and made an inquiry of my hon. friend. What did he say when I spoke of the matter?
Despatch from Guelph, Ontario, October 22:
"No munitions," said Hon. Hugh Guthrie, Minister of Militia, at one o'clock this morning, "have been purchased since the war excepting a few spare parts to put in shape such material as we have in Canada."
And in further correspondence I had with the then Prime Minister and the Minister of Militia, which correspondence I shall ask to have brought down so that every hon. member may have the privilege of reading it, they admitted that these high explosive shells were paid for out of a credit to Canada's account in England. What is a credit? It is the same as an appropriation by Parliament. It represents the money of the people of the country ; it represents what the people have paid out in the form of taxation one way or another. It is out of that money that
this $2,879,453 worth of high explosive shells has been paid. What is to be done with these shells? Of the shells I saw, every box was marked " To be fired or destroyed before June 1925 otherwise they would be of no value. My information went to show that these shells have been sent all over the country, deposited not in one province but in half a dozen provinces; and I am told, I believe rightly, that the only place in Canada where the militia would think of firing them is the camp at Petawawa where the artillery practise. Whether I am right or wrong in that regard I stand ready to be corrected. But the point is this: we have bought, according to government records, a couple of million dollars' worth of high explosive shells, representing one-fifth of the whole appropriation which is asked for the department for this year. What are we to do with these shells? I am told that they are no good for ordinary practice; and they must be destroyed, according to the indications on the boxes themselves, within a certain period. I shall place on record the statement my hon. friend gave me, and which came from his department, when I wrote him inquiring what had been ordered. This is only a part of the quantity that has been imported. Earlier in the same year, as far back as July 15, 1920, I find that there was an importation of shells and cartridges to the value of $355,865. Not a word was said to this Parliament about any shells or cartridges having been brought from England at that time, but Parliament was asked to vote money in order that this very class of thing might be purchased from the arsenals in Canada which, according to the statement of my hon. friend, made all the heavy artillery munitions. Let me refer to the first matter. My hon. friend has put forward what, in my judgment, is a very, very, lame excuse for the language he used this afternoon. He has not attempted to justify it. I am going to put myself in the judgment of the House in regard to this whole incident. But when a man in the position, and of the ability, and intelligence, of my hon. friend puts forward the lame excuse in this House, that the trouble arose because he always believed demobilization was the opposite of mobilization, and consequently was misled by something I said, such an excuse is ridiculous. He sat within twelve or thirteen feet of me, when I explained to him every particular, every item, told him where every man was both here and overseas. Does he insinuate that he moved to reduce this item because he was misled, because he thought the demobilization was still going on and was completed? It would have been much more fair, much more candid on his part, much more manly, I think also if he had told the House: I did make that motion to reduce this item in 1920 just for the reasons that are stated in Hansard, and I was not misled. But I am going to leave myself entirely in the judgment of the House and let the House decide upon a review of all the facts. However, such is the lame excuse which the Prime Minister puts forward to justify his change of front. He has turned some sharp corners this session,-perhaps this is the sharpest corner he has had to turn. I still think the manly way would have been the best way for him to have explained his difficult position.
Now, in regard to the other matter, I absolutely deny the charge that I in any way misled or deceived the House in regard to ammunition shipments and had my hon. friend, the Prime Minister, not gone to Levis and become alarmed and over excited at what he saw there, we never would have

Supply-Militia
had this tremendous ado about something which is capable of a very simple and very satisfactory explanation. The explanation has been given to my hon. friend by me in written form, but he has not seen fit to use it to-night. Even after he received that explanation during the late campaign he did not see fit to use it, but he went from platform to platform shouting at the top of his voice as he did in the city of Guelph according to the report in the Toronto Globe: This ammunition matter constitutes one of the gravest political scandals, if not one of the gravest political crimes, that was ever committed in the Dominion of Canada.
Hear, hear.

There are a good many "hear hears" by members who don't understand and I am going to explain the matter briefly to the House. The shell transaction took place before I became Minister of Militia, but I do not seek to shield myself on that account. I have concerned myself enough about it to make inquiries from Sir Edward Kemp, who was at that time Overseas Minister of Militia, and also of my hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) my predecessor in oifice, in whose time the (whole transaction took place. I have also gone to the trouble of ascertaining definitely from the Deputy Minister of the Department-who is present on the floor to-night-and from the chief of the general staff, who was personally concerned with the matter, all the facts I could possibly gather.
When I stated in the newspaper interview quoted by my hon. friend and which I gave over the telephone at one o'clock in the morning, that no ammunition had been purchased since the armistice down to date, I said what was absolutely true, or else the officials in my department had not told me all that was going on. The statement was absolutely true-not a dollar's worth of ammunition had been bought. Ammunition had certainly been manufactured in the government arsenals but none had been purchased since the armistice.
How did this matter arise? When the armistice came, it came suddenly. Canada, like the other allied nations, did not know there was going to be a sudden cessation of hostilities on November 11. We, like the other allied nations, were preparing for a year or two years more of war, and we were accumulating large stocks of warlike material of every kind-guns, ammunition, shells, all kinds of military equipment, clothes, medical stores and the like, and when the armistice came we had tremendous quantities of all kinds of military supplies on hand in France, in Belgium and in Great Britain; we had also a tremendous supply in Canada.
Let me deal first with the supplies overseas. The practical question immediately arose: What are we going to do with all these stores? How shall we dispose of them? In ordinary peace times our militia could not use them in a generation, no, I have been told by the officers of the department that we could not use them in two or three generations. A great deal of that war material will deteriorate by lapse of time just as in the case of these high explosive shells which so alarmed the Prime Minister, and which bore on the containers instructions that they were to be used before a certain fixed date, otherwise they would go bad, and be of no use whatever.
What then were we to do with this large accumulation of warlike stores? There is the technical and proper term, and that is the term I have used from time to time in this House, What was Australia doing ? What was New Zealand doing? They could not use their tremendous accumulations, nor could we use ours. We simply pooled them all. We all turned our warlike stores over to the British government, and the British government took records of them and agreed to store them for us until some final disposition could be decided upon. We knew we could make use of some of them in our militia in Canada, and the overseas ministry, presided over at that time by Sir Edward Kemp, and. General MaoBrien, one of the most capable officers this country has ever turned out, and with some others, acting on behalf of Canada, determined that the best course to take was to withdraw from this tremendous surplus store of our own supplies what we could utilize in militia training in Canada. Thereupon lists were prepared of such part of that military equipment, including guns, munitions and all kinds of warlike stores, which it was considered we could use in this country. After these lists were prepared and submitted to the British War Office, they said in regard to guns: We will hand over to you absolutely new guns to take the place of your guns which have seen service, because we have a tremendous stock of new guns on hand, and we will take yours over at inventory prices. For use of those guns we selected a supply of appropriate ammunition.

If one branch of military science has been developed during the war more than another it was the artillery branch of the service. Guns which we were using in Canada at the beginning of the war became absolutely useless as the war progressed. We had to have new modern guns. New guns require new ammunition high explosive ammunition-and such ammunition had not previously been manufactured at any of our government arsenals. What was the use of eighteen pounder high explosive guns if you had no high explosive shells? We had the guns, and we drew out of the general pool as part of our share a sufficient quantity of shells for those guns for the use of our millitia troops in annual training.
Will my hon. friend allow me a question? Do I understand him to say that no high explosive shells, either of the eighteen pounder or higher calibres, were manufactured in Canada?

None were manufactured in our arsenals. We had no machinery for the manufacture of them, so the Superintendent of Arsenals has reported. I understand such shells were made in Canada by some of the munition plants, but I am talking of the government arsenals. We drew out such material as we could reasonably use, and I admit that to the ordinary civilian mind the list appears to be a pretty long one, but if the hon. Prime Minister will consult the Minister of Militia, or the Deputy Minister, or the Chief of Staff, I think he will find that under modern war conditions we had a reserve of just one day's artillery supplies in this country. That is what we have-one single day's supplies. I have received a written memorandum from the Chief of Staff to this effect. It is not a very heavy supply of reserve artillery ammunition under modern war conditions, is it? I do not understand the technique in many of these matters, and therefore I have to be guided by what competent officers tell me, and such is the information I have received, upon very high authority.
Well, we selected what was coming to us, or rather what General MacBrien and his committee of officers in England thought was proper for us to have for militia training. My colleague, the then Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewburn), and the Overseas Minister of Militia, Sir Edward Kemp, both agreed upon the matter, and the question then was: How were we to ship it out to Canada? Immediately after the war we

could not get shipping, but as shipping later became available all of this war material, including guns, ammunition, and all kinds of military equipment, was from time to time sent forward to Canada. There was a great lot of it we could never use in Canada. What did we do with the surplus? We were in a bad fix in regard to a lot of our equipment unless some other government would take it over. We could never use it in Canada. Finally the British government agreed to take the whole surplus off our hands. A valuation was made of it, and the War Office allowed us,
I think, three million dollars or thereabouts for the balance of our equipment which we did not desire to bring back to Canada. It was all purely a question of salvage. What,
I ask, was the best thing to do under all the circumstances. Was it not better to sell the surplus to the War Office and bring back to this country such portion as we could reasonably use? Many of the guns which we decided to bring back had never been seen in Canada before, or, indeed, any guns like them. The ammunition for these guns had never been in Canada before, or anything like them. Bringing the guns, we would need the ammunition. My hon. friend the Prime Minister in some of his speeches assured his audience that some officer in Ottawa had told him that high explosive shells were never used in artillery practice or training. If he had gone to Pete-wawa or Sarcee or Camp Hughes in 1921 when the troops were there, he would have found them firing 18-pounder high explosive shells. If he had gone to Pete-wawa last year he would have found the same thing, and if he will go there this year when the artillery is in training he will see our troops firing the identical shells that he saw landed at Quebec last October, brought here for the purpose of training the Canadian militia. What were we to do with our surplus war material if we did not use it in that way? We used what we could-we saved that money to the country, because otherwise we would have had to purchase or manufacture additional war material-and what we could not use in our militia we got the government of Great Britain to take off our hands at a valuation of $3,000,000. In addition, of course, we had on hand this tremendous supply of war material here in Canada, sufficient to carry on the militia of this country for thirty or forty years under peace conditions. We did the very same thing in Canada as we did in England; we

Supply-Militia
selected out of these unused stores as much as we could reasonably utilize in our militia before it should rot or become worn out through old age, and we stored it in the various depots throughout Canada. But there was a large surplus which we could	not use in	many years
and we handed this surplus over to the War Purchasing Commission, who sold it for the best price obtainable-something like seven or eight millions of dollars.
This is the story of the so-called shell scandal, and that is the whole of it. That is the story of the shipment of shells which so excited my hon. friend the Prime Minister during the late campaign. Is there anything wrong about it? There is a little quibble about a word in Hansard; perhaps I had better explain that circumstance. In recent years we have maintained two arsenals, one at Quebec, which is equipped with machinery to turn out certain kinds of artillery and rifle ammunition; another at Lindsay, Ontario, where rifle ammunition only is manufactured- this is the only kind of ammunition which the machinery there will produce. Certain kinds of artillery ammunition can be made at Quebec. All the artillery ammunition which we manufacture in Canada we do make at Quebec; none of the artillery ammunition made in Canada is made at Lindsay. That is the idea which I intended to convey in the language I used as quoted to-night by the Prime Minister. I was asked how many men were employed at the various arsenals and what were they making, and I said: " All the artillery ammunition is made at Quebec." I should have said: All that we make in Canada is made at Quebec; none is made at Lindsay. But it is upon that mere quibble, upon that single word, my hon. friend the Prime Minister has had the effrontery to get up in this House and rest his whole case.
May I explain again the matter of the demobilization vote. During the war none of our war expenditure was charged to the Militia Department; it would not have been fair to so charge it. While active hostilities were proceeding, all such expenditure was charged to a vote called " war appropriation." All supplies, all stores, all guns, all transport-everything was charged to the war appropriation vote, nothing to the Militia Department. We were at war; it was war money we were spending, and a special report of the expenditure from time to time was laid on the table of the House giving every item in detail. I myself laid either one or two
such reports on the Table, and i 9 p.m. they are still available. At the end of the war we adopted a special vote called the demobilization vote. By act of this Parliament we defined what " demobilization" should include. This act is 9-10 George V, chapter 33. It provided that a certain sum should be appropriated not exceeding $250,000,000, towards defraying any expenses incurred by or under the authority of the Governor in Council during the year ending March 31, 1920, for the following purposes:
(a)	the defence and security of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naval and military operations in or beyond Canada and the demobilization of the Canadian forces;
(c)	the promoting of trade and industry, and transportation facilities therefor;
(d)	the carrying out of any measures deemed necessary or advisable by the Governor in Council in consequence of the war; and
(e)	payments made or expenditure incurred during the fiscal year ending the thirty-first day of March, nineteen hundred and nineteen, for the purposes mentioned in The War Appropriation Act, 1918, and in excess of the amount authorized by the said act.
That act passed for the first time in 1919, and, I think, was re-enacted the following year and, the next year again in the Appropriation Act. Yet a man of the intelligence and parliamentary experience of the Prime Minister of this country comes before the House to-night and tries to lead the House to believe that he did not know what the demobilization vote was. Well, there is the statute. Why did he not read it? I have no doubt he heard it discussed in the House at least twenty times during each session; since it was passed. The demobilization vote was a continual subject of discussion. I think my hon. friend himself was here in the session of 1919, when the act was passed. Surely his professed ignorance as to what demobilization included makes the excuse he has tried to offer in regard to my first objection a very lame one indeed.
Now, I have given a full account of the "shell scandal" from the point of view of the Government of that day. All the records in connection with the whole transaction are in the Militia Department. The overseas papers are all in Canada now; the overseas minister relinquished his office some time before the Government was defeated and his records will be found in the department. All the particulars are there, and the Prime Minister, if he wishes to do so, can delve into them to the bottom. The same officers are in the department to-day as were there when I was in office, and full information
Supply-Militia

can be had from them. If my hon. friend can find anything wrong in the transaction, anything unbusinesslike in the transaction, anything deceitful in the transaction, let him find it, and make it known to the House. I for one am prepared to say that in anything the Militia Department did in that connection it acted wisely and in the interests of the people, and the Government did wisely to conclude the arrangement with the British War Office which I have outlined and brought that ammunition back to Canada and saved the expense of buying it in the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wish to prolong this discussion unduly, because I think this matter will be better threshed out before the Public Accounts Committee. And I hope the committee will look into it; I am sure that the papers to which my hon. friend has referred will bear examination. When my hon. friend uses the word "effrontery," I think he had better have some regard to his own behaviour. After listening to the explanation he has made of the bringing in of these thirteen or fourteen shiploads of high explosive shells, the House will not have very much difficulty in finding a characterization that will be suitable for his action. When he talks about being manly, I think he might have discarded the lame excuse he laboured under at the outset of intimating that this matter came under his predecessor in office, an hon. gentleman who did not happen to be in the Chamber at the time but who sits beside my hon. friend on other occasions. Every word I read to the House to-night was from the lips of my hon. friend. They were not the words of his predecessor; they were his own words. He has not touched the point of deception which I brought up, which was this: If he knew, as he said he did, that Canada was entitled to these shiploads of shells, why did he not tell Parliament that at tba last session, when he was asking us to appropriate money for the purposes of munitions?
Why did he not the year before, if he knew this country was entitled to munitions amounting to $6,000,000 or more from the other side,-why did he not tell Parliament then? I tell my hon. friend that the people of this country will not believe that it was a mere matter of accident that he did not tell this House that we were entitled to all this quantity of ammunition from the other side if we were so entitled. That will not go down with the people of Canada, and my hon. friend would be the last person

to accept any such statement from anyone else that might happen to make it. Altogether, there were I think thirteen or fourteen {Merchant [Marine shiploads of these shells brought into this country. My hon. friend says that they were all obligated for during the time that his predecessor was in office. According to his statement he knew that, and yet he told the House absolutely nothing about it, but came before the House and asked to vote a sum of money for artillery ammunition, telling us that all the artillery ammunition was made in this country and that the money was needed on that account. All of the shells that came in have come in since the debate in which my hon. friend made his statement to the House.
Now in regard to these being our stores, it may be perfectly true, as was said, that there was a certain pooling of supplies after the armistice and that Canada was entitled to draw what she needed out of that pool, but there was a financial settlement made later, according to the Prime Minister and the Minister of
10 p.m. Militia himself, which placed to Canada's account a certain credit. That credit represented the money of the people of, this country, and if I am not wrongly informed, I think the minister's letter will show that these shells have come out of that credit. He talks about our own stores. If these shells to the extent of $6,000,000 or more in value, had not been brought in Canada would have had to its credit $6,000,000 more on the other side.

How? That was our
equipment. How would we have had $6,000,000 for it?

Was there

It comes
