All we had in Canada
that we could not utilize we handed over to the Purchasing Commission, and they sold it for approximately $7,000,000 or $8,000,000. All we had in England that we considered we could utilize in our militia we brought back to Canada and what we could not utilize, we sold to the British government for about $3,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I said,
I think this is a matter that can be better gone into and threshed out by a committee than at this particular moment. My hon. friends may smile, but I think it is still owing to this House that the ex-Minister of Militia should explain why, if Canada was entitled to these supplies, if she had them in her possession at the time, he told this Parliament .nothing about it. He should also explain why he asked of this Parliament, and accepted from this Parliament, appropriations for the purchase of munitions when, according to his present statement, we had these very munitions in our possession.
I wish to say this further, and I think this is a matter that can be decided at the present time irrespective of anything else: The quantity of high explosive shells that he has brought into this country is far in excess of any use that can possibly be made of them by the militia of this country. Apart from the questionable nature of the transaction, these shells have cost us an enormous sum in the matter of transportation and distribution. They are costing this country at the present time a large sum on account of inspection and storage, and I venture to say that they will not be used but will be destroyed before the time for which they are due. Now perhaps my hon. friend will tell the House just why he said nothing whatever about any munitions to which we were entitled when he was asking us to vote money for munitions and when he knew that after his appropriations had
passed he was going to bring in ship loads of these munitions.
When the vote for munitions came up, I did inform the House that a certain amount of military stores- that would include munitions-
Oh, oh.

Well would it not? On one occasion I defined what the term military stores included. The vote I asked from the House was fully explained, in the printed estimates last year, a copy of which I hold in my hand, just as it is explained in the estimates this year. You will find in those estimates specifications of every kind of ammunition for which the vote was taken, just as you find it for this year. What we selected in England was largely what we did not have in Canada, and what we did not propose to manufacture here. A very large part of it is what we could not make with our present equipment. I suppose, had I been specifically asked whether the term military stores included ammunition I could have said yes. I certainly mentioned guns, and I think I described some of them. I certainly mentioned other military equipment, but I was not asked specifically in regard to shells. When I presented the estimates and asked for the vote, I gave the exact specifications of what we proposed to make with the money Parliament voted to us, just as it is set forth in the estimates to-day.

May I respectfully suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the discussion which has been going on for nearly an hour has been out of order and could have been held much better under another item, that of Ordnance, Arms, etc.
The item which we are at present discussing is an item of $1,400,000 to be devoted to annual drill and training of the militia. Last year when this item came before the House, the then member for Kent, now a member of another House, moved that the item be reduced by the amount of $750,000. At that time a largo number of members now sitting on this side of the House supported the motion of the hon. member for Kent that $750,000 be struck from the vote. In order to be fair to the government of that day, we thought that $750,000 was a lot to ask a Tory government to take from military expenditure, but to-day the Government in power is supported by members who, at any rate during the last campaign when they were
Supply-Militia

in opposition, announced that they were anti-militarists. In order to give them and the Government an opportunity of showing that the principle which they advocated in opposition will be the same principle which they advocate when in power. I move, seconded by my hon. friend from Laprairie (Mr. Lanctot), that this item be reduced by $1,100,000. I would move that it be reduced by the sum total of the vote, but perhaps there may be some small outstanding accounts which require to be paid, and I would not wish to deprive any of the citizens of Canada of their just recourse against the Government in case there is any money	due.
In moving this amendment to the resolution I would suggest that we are opposed to such ian expenditure because, in the first place, we have no money for such a purpose. We have been told time and again by the members of the Opposition and by our friends the Progressives that the country is on the verge of bankruptcy. If such is the case we surely have no means that will permit us to indulge in useless expenditure, and expenditure on militia camps, or for military training, at the present time is, to my mind, a useless expenditure. I understand from the minister that we have reduced the period of training from sixteen to nine days. I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that nine days' training is not sufficient for the making of a soldier and cannot be of any use for that purpose. We heard last year from distinguished soldiers -the then member for Skeena, Mr. Peck, the then member for Edmonton Mr. Gries-bach, and others, who have held high rank in the army that it took six months steady, continuous and intensive training to make a man fit to be placed on the fighting line. I submit that nine days training-one day of which is spent in going to, and one day in returning from, the camp, while Sunday is devoted to church parades in any God fearing province-means that we really have only six days in which to teach men to form fours. That, I think, is not sufficient and I submit it is not in the best interest of the country that we waste our money in merely giving a holiday to those who can find any useful employment in the country.
I would go further and say that there is no necessity, even though it were useful, for such military training to-day. It was pointed out by my hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. Gould) that in these days we hear nothing but reports of peace conferences on disarmament, and we spent some thoust*Ir. Power.]
ands of dollars in sending a representative to the Disarmament Conference in Washington. The whole world is talking of disarmament, and we have treaties between the most important powers tending to that end. As has been pointed out for years by members on this side, we are in no immediate danger from any enemy. Last year the then Minister of Militia stated that the militia estimates had been cut down to the lowest point consistent with safety. I repeatedly asked him the question-safety from what, safety from whom? From whom are we liable to attack? Who is about to attack us? The minister could not give me a reply at that time; and I do not know that he can give me a reply to-day. I think it is well known and clearly understood that there is no immediate danger of this country being attacked; that we do not need to at once begin to train the youth of Canada, and that further, the training of young people in the usages and the glorification of war will do more to make new wars than any other propaganda. I say, Sir, that if you teach the youth of this country to use arms, that if you constantly hold before them that the supreme and the sovereign means of settling any difficulty is by the arbitrary method of force, you will lead them to the conclusion that there is no means of obtaining truth and justice in this world but by the use of force. So that for the three reasons I have mentioned:	First, because we have no
money; second, because such training would be useless, and, third, because there is no necessity for it, I very reluctantly-because I think the members of the House who know me realize that I am a very strong party man; I believe in party government, and I believe in Liberal party government above all party governments, I am very reluctantly obliged in order to be consistent with my stand on former occasions and with what I have said throughout the country and particularly in my own constituency during the last election, to ask for this reduction in the estimates.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question is on
the amendment moved by Mr. Power that the item of $1,400,000 for annual drill be reduced by $1,100,000. Shall the amendment carry?

I would1 like to ask the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, if it would not be possible-in view of the reduction in the cost of living, in view of the increased purchasing power of the dollar, and in view of the fact to which my hon. friend from South Wellingt m (Mr. Guthrie) has already referred, that this decrease is more apparent than real-to reduce this item of $1,400,000 by $400,000. I think we might perhaps agree on a compromise of that kind. I make the suggestion because I have in my possession, as the Minister for Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. Beland) is already aware letters from men who have recently developed tubercular trouble but who are not considered eligible to make any claim for
remuneration. I am of opinion-and I should like to test the committee in this matter-that this money could be better spent in looking after the fatherless, the widows, and disabled soldiers who were stricken and maimed in the great conflict than spent in this way. In view of what I have stated, I think this item of $1,400,000 could be reduced by $400,000, and I do not think anybody would suffer in the interval. Our paramount duty at the moment is not to provide for the training of men until we have seen to it that men disabled in the great conflict are adequately looked after.

I have noticed with some interest the co-operation which is taking place between the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) and the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Graham). What one says the other appears to corroborate. Incidentally, even when the civil government estimates of the department were before the House, I was quite interested in noting that the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence tendered his services to the present Minister of Militia and Defence, advising that the list was complete; that it had been reduced to the lowest possible point. It seems to me that we in this House should ask the question: Who are the advisers of the minister? As a matter of fact, I have asked questions, similar to this on several previous occasions, while the civil government estimates have been before the House. There must be, in the Government or in the various departments, individuals who advise the min-, isters, and it seems to me that the time has arrived, in the annual protest which we make on the floor of this House against gross expenditures of money, when we must issue notice to those individuals who advise the ministers in their departments, that there is, throughout the country, a strict demand for economy, and that the people are going to see that they themselves who furnish this money have representatives or advisers in connection with the spending of that money, who know the position thoroughly. That is, the individuals who are the advisers must take the dual position of understanding the stand of the people who furnish the money as well as of understanding the spending of the money. This is not a newly-found fault or idea with me. It appears to me that the individuals who advise have said unto themselves: "Oh, well, Parliament will provide the money; all we have to do is to find the
Supply-Militia

means of spending it," and they have not had a proper conception of the attitude of mind of the people who, away back home, are watching the activities of the people here, and who are wondering if those whom they have sent to Parliament are going to vote these huge sums of money simply upon the request of those who are, perhaps, the advisers of the ministers.
I recollect a question which I asked last year of the then Minister of Militia and Defence. My question which had to do with Military District No. 12, which is located in Saskatchewan, was if it was the intention of the minister to discontinue Military District No. 12? My question was prompted by the fact that this district had been established during the war period upon the distinct understanding and promise that it would be discontinued immediately upon the termination of the war. The Minister of Militia and Defence replied to my question by stating that Saskatchewan had proved to be such a good recruiting ground that they had decided to keep the district in operation. It was news to me and to the people back home that the part of this country from which I come, supposedly at that time filled with Bolshevists, should be accounted by the Minister of Militia and Defence as a good recruiting ground. Certainly, that was an inconsistent position, and we are justified in assuming and believing, from the reply of the minister, that he was capable, in that respect, of taking a somewhat dual attitude. That military district is still in existence, and I have some figures which I wish to place on Hansard, not particularly for the benefit of the gentlemen in this chamber, but for the people back home who will tomorrow read Hansard. I have made complaints on the public platform that I thought there was extravagance in this department, and I want to cite a few figures in relation to Military District No. 12. I have stated on the public platform that I believe an undue proportion of the moneys voted was going to officers, and I have in my hand figures to show the proportion. In Military District No. 12, that is in Saskatchewan, we have:
18th Battery, C.F.A., 3 officers, 3 N.C.O's, 19 men.
31st Battery, C.F.A., 4 officers, 7 N.C.O's, 42 men.
44th Battery, C.F.A., 4 officers, 8 N.C.O's, 43 men.
77th Battery, C.F.A., 3 officers, 9 N.C.O's, 85 men.
12th Brigade, C.M.G., Headquarters staff, 4 officers, 1 N.C.O. ; No. 1 Company, 2 officers, 7

N.C.O's; No. 2 Company, 6 officers, 5 N.C.O's, 13 men ; No. 3 Company, 5 officers, 8 N.C.O's, 60 men.
12th Signal Company, C.S.C., 5 officers, 11
N.C.O's, 57 men.
I might say that the other military districts, in many cases, show the same proportion, and, in my humble opinion there are far too many officers for the number of men shown. I think I stated last year that they average practically one officer to every two men, and we are being asked to provide money for salaries for those officers.
The economic condition of this country does not warrant such expenditure, and the people have given a distinct mandate to us, who represent them on this floor, that they will no longer abide by the decision of those who advise the minister to ask for huge sums of money to be voted to provide for these inordinate expenditures. I have made repeated protests on the floor of this House; soon I hope to see the fruits of my labour and the co-operation of others who have worked with me, in the reduction of the estimates of this department of Government. I am pleased to link my forces with those of the hon. and gallant member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) when he asks for a reduction in these estimates. I am very sure that, under the present economic conditions of this country, under the wish and will of the people, expressed because of the promises made throughout the length and breadth of Canada by us who asked that the confidence of the people be reposed in us, the time has arrived when the people have a right, in this first meeting of a new Parliament, to demand that these expenditures should be reduced. Consequently, I feel obliged to vote for the adoption of the amendment.

It is rather an unusual spectacle to find the Government in discussion over a certain matter with its own friends, and the situation was made even more interesting this afternoon when it was found that the Government, on this point, was receiving support from members of the official opposition. But that is a situation which is likely to arise when we have a sudden change in government. Hard as the new administration may strive to drive away from the methods of the old regime, yet members on this side may find that they are not driving fast enough, and they may ask for more radical reforms. I quite understand the position in which the minister finds himself. When he took charge of the office he found an established department, an established staff, and fixed

Supply-Militia
customs. And I will give him credit for the fact that he at once proceeded to use the pruning knife and was able to announce that he would reduce his estimates this year by over a million dollars. The significance of this reduction is fully apparent when it is remembered that he has to meet statutory increases in salaries, ranging as high as half a million dollars. If we recall, however, that not later than twelve months ago we on this side moved to reduce a similar estimate by 50 per cent, the Government must not be surprised if it finds, even on this side of the House, some members asking for a substantial reduction. There is no sort of economy more to the liking of the people than any saving that can be effected in the Department of Militia, unless it be in the Department of Naval Service. I heard this afternoon, in regard to this item, the argument that after all we are not spending more than we did in 1910, because the value of the Canadian dollar has depreciated. Well, we must bear in mind, along with that fact, the different conditions that existed in 1910. Then we were rich and prosperous; we had surpluses and could spend, not only on urgent matters but also on useful works even though they were not of immediate necessity. Such is not the case now. Last year we had to face deficits amounting to some $200,000,000, and although the Government this year has reduced expenses to a large extent, I regret that the revenue of the country is also decreasing; and it is possible after all that the balance sheet this year may be similar to the one we had last year. I say, therefore, that we cannot use that argument, that we are not spending more than we did in 1910, because the value of the Canadian dollar has dropped. What would you think of a business man who would argue that because he spent $15,000 some ten years ago, when his business was prosperous, he must spend $25,000 this year, when he faces bankruptcy, simply because the value of the dollar has gone down?
With regard to the matter of annual drill, I do not think we can consider this an essential part of the regular departmental work. I know that many members of the force are of the opinion that these drills in the country during the summer time are mere camp feasts or holidays, and I think it would be only proper if the holiday this year were enjoyed by the taxpayers. 1 am not prejudiced; I will not commit myself as regards the future; but I must say that unless a stronger argument is advanced for the maintenance of this
particular institution I shall have to vote for a reduction of the vote.

Prior to the last Dominion election a certain newspaper published in this country made the prophecy that the Progressive party might not be the dog that would do the barking at Ottawa for the next three or four years, but would be at least the tail that would wag the dog. It seems to me that the tail is beginning to wag the dog just a little bit away from the old bone of contention back to the real issue before the House in the consideration of these estimates. I desire to ally myself with the motion that has been made across the floor reducing the amount from $1,400,000 to the handsome sum of $300,000. Even $300,000 is a large sum of money for this purpose, when we consider item No. 51, at page 22 of the estimates, which provides for seed, feed and fertilizer control only the sum of $275,000. I was in our western country during the Easter recess and saw some of the conditions as they exist there this spring among the farmers of my own constituency. I found more than one bank closed and the farmers unable to get loans to buy seed. More than one farmer came to me personally and asked if I would finance him to buy seed because he could not be accommodated through the banks. Yet here in our estimates we find only the small sum of $275,000 apportioned by the Parliament of Canada to the business of financing the people for seed for the important industry of agriculture. I submit that agriculture is of far more importance to the Dominion of Canada than the matter of annual drill, which includes pay, subsistence and allowances to officers and men of the active militia during training, as well as transportation and other local expenses. I think that the few thousand men who will profit by this allowance of $300,000, if the amendment carries, are a small body indeed compared with the several hundred thousand men who came from the agricultural lands of this Dominion and showed their worth during the late war.

If I understand the principle of responsible government, it is the duty of the Minister of Mi'litia and the Prime Minister, and other members of the Cabinet, to defend this vote of $1,400,000 which they have recommended to Parliament. In 1920 there was voted; by the House for annual drill, etc., $12,500,000, only $10,000,000 of which was spent. The reason the other $2,500,000 was not spent

Supply-Militia

was that only the city units were drilled at their headquarters. It is all very well for my friends on my left to bring in an amendment like this and think it is economy. It is false economy and not in the interests of the people of this country.
Let me correct the hon. member. The motion to reduce the vote was not moved by hon. members to his left.

I am glad to hear my hon. friend make the correction, but some of the sentiments expressed by hon. gentlemen of his party endorse the sentiment of the amendment. Now, Mr. Chairman, I think we are at the parting of the ways in this country in regard to militia matters. If this motion to reduce the vote were carried we might as well close up the Militia Department altogether, and it would be a sorry day for the people of Canada if that were done, not only for Quebec but for Ontario and other parts of the country as well. As I have said, the reason why the balance of the appropriation of $12,500,000, amounting to $2,500,000, was not spent in 1920 was the fact that after the war it was difficult to organize and put on a peace footing what might be termed the country regiments. The $10,000,000 expended was largely spent in drilling city corps of the large cities like Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, London, Halifax, Winnipeg, Vancouver, etc. It was devoted to what you might call the city units in the various military districts in Canada. With the small amount of money voted last year the minister reopened the military training camps from coast to coast for the country corps. I attended the Niagara camp at the request of the commanding officer, and I cannot speak too highly of the work done there by the units in training, but I was surprised to hear the discontent among the men both of the rural and the city battalions. Some of the officers of a very fine battalion, the 31st of Grey, then under the command of Colonel Carmichael, a member of the Drury Government, and an excellent soldier and officer, told me that the returned men were getting disgusted at the cheap way the camp was run. The militia estimates were cut down, necessitating the units putting their hands in their pockets to keep things going. I heard the same complaint from men from my own city. The company funds were all exhausted during the war. The 13th battalion, formerly under the command of that fine soldier and patriot-my hon. friend from 
East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn), handed over $30,000 of their funds for the recruiting of their war regiments. In a word, the various militia units after the war were bankrupt. I think 206 units attended the camps last June, and the officers who raised those units brought them into camp only 20 to 25 per cent strong because of the insufficient allowances and expenditure by the Militia Department.
I do not say it is the fault of any particular person or party, but, after all is said and done, we must keep up our defensive forces, and if any one doubts the wisdom of this he has only to go back to 1812, when we are told General Brock could not induce the old legislative assembly to grant him sufficient funds to defend the country. What would have happened to Canada if we had had no militia at that time? The legislative assembly then cut down the estimates for annual drills and defence with the result that General Brock got disgusted and is said to have written to the authorities at home requesting to be recalled. A debate similar to the present one took place in 1911, 1912, and 1913, in this House on militia estimates.
I venture to say, that more than 80 per cent of the men from Toronto in the first contingent for overseas were men who belonged to the militia, and had it not been for the military training they had received from militia units the late Sir Sam Hughes would not have been able to send over our first contingent of 30,000 men within a few months after the outbreak of war. The value of preparedness has been demonstrated over and over again; indeed, it has been stated by many eminent military experts that if the British Empire had been as well prepared on land as on sea in 1914 we would have had no war at all.
If we are to have any militia force at all we must have annual training camps, and it is undisputed that those camps today are not what they should be. The money spent on these annual camps is wisely spent, but if you whittle down this vote too much you might as well throw the money into the Ottawa river for all the good its expenditure would accomplish, as it would be inadequate to produce proper results. I do not believe the people either of Quebec or any other province are asking for this reduction. It is false economy and not true economy to reduce this vote, and I hope the Minister of Militia and the other members of the Government will arise and defend the item, as

Supply-Militia
responsible government in my view requires them to do so.
Objection has been raised that these camps inculcate a military spirit. Well, in the days of stress and strain when the war broke out was it not a good thing that we had plenty of young men imbued with that military spirit? If not, we would have cut a sorry figure in the war and in recruiting and Canada would never have rendered the service she did to the Mother Country and to civilization.

I am sure every member fully appreciates what was done by the Militia Department during the war, and by our young men who enlisted and went overseas. But to-day we are trying to get away from war conditions, we are trying to re-establish ourselves on a peace footing. As a young member a couple of sessions ago I listened with a good deal of interest to our delegates who had attended the Peace Conference while they told us that the signing of the Peace Treaty was to end war for all time to come. We were encouraged to believe from what they said that the day had come when swords would be beaten into ploughshares and spears into pruning-hooks. I am sure we will rejoice at the dawn of a new day when disputes between nations will be settled by ballots and conferences instead of bloodshed and slaughter. Now, we have spent as Canadians a great deal of money in connection with peace conferences and conferences on the reduction of armaments, and some are wondering if we cannot reduce very largely the expenditure on the militia for a year or two in order to pay the expenses of peace conferences and peace treaties. If we are going to have peace I do not think it is a good sign to prepare for war. I do not anticipate a war in the near future, and I do not think anyone else in Canada does. If any trouble is apprehended, then our peace conferences and our negotiations for the reduction of armaments are all in vain. I think the time has come when we should devote more attention to preparing for peace and reestablishing peace than preparing for war. Now, we appreciate the militia just as much as many other people who are advocating it so strongly to-night. The member for North Toronto seems to be terribly excited over the thought that if this vote is not granted the militia will go to pieces and Canada will have no protection. Now, we have a great many trained men in Canada to-day, and in view of the present
75J
financial condition of the country we were wondering if some saving could not be made. That is the reason why some of the members on both sides are talking about this reduction.
When my hon. friend says there are a large number of trained men, I assume he refers to the men who fought at the front.
Yes.

Is it the hon. member's suggestion that in the event of trouble -and God forbid that we should have trouble-we should call on these men who went through four years of hell and ask them to do this duty again instead of its being done by newly trained men?

We are not looking
for war, we are preparing for peace, and we are spending money for that purpose. We have men going over to peace conferences with a view of preparing for peace. T may say that I had perhaps as many friends in khaki as the hon. gentleman had, so I am not speaking from that point of view. I say I respect the militia; we want the militia, but this is a time when retrenchment is necessary. In the minister's opinion, if the military drill for this year were postponed, would it to a great extent decrease the efficiency of. our militia, and what would the saving be? The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who is opposed to militarism, has told us that this training is for a period of six days. Well, I really do not think the absence of six days' training would affect the efficiency of the militia of Canada, which has been trained for so long. I really do not think it would for one year, but I want the minister's opinion on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The object is not to continue the training of the boys who were overseas, but to use the officers who received that training to train new young men. I would not ask this House to vote one cent for the further training of the boys who have been trained overseas; I want to give them a rest. The suggestion that the annual drill is for a period of six days, or, in the case of the city corps, nine days, does not leave a fair impression. Some of these men might be trained a good deal longer than they get paid for training, the idea being to keep up their efficiency. My Chief of Staff, General MacBrien, who is a level-headed man and has given great service to the country,
Supply-Militia

does not, as has been suggested, make his living in the Militia Department; he loves the work and has been selected above a great many for the position. Ten days ago I put the question squarely to him: If we cut out military training for one year what effect would it have? He said: "The effect would be disastrous on any attempt to maintain an organization of voluntary militia throughout the Dominion of Canada." That is the reply he gave me. I have no desire to spend the people's money, but hon. gentlemen talking of economy should remember that some economy has been practised. I venture the assertion that there has been more economy in the cutting of these estimates than has been exercised by any business man in the House in connection with his annual expenditure during the past year. The department has been established since the war on a basis of efficiency and strength by men who have served overseas. On going into a department, the minister, of course, has his own difficulties as well as the officers. But I want to remove an impression which has been created: the officers of the Militia Department have given me every assistance. If hon. members knew the men of whom I speak, they would resent some of the things that are said about them. They are men of practical experience in military matters, and very good business men, some of them. Now, the purpose of the motion is to do away with the annual drill, and if it were adopted I would look for a general degeneration, if not an entire wiping out, of the militia spirit on the part of the young men-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Now, I do not like to hear that applause within four years of the time when we applauded so many of our young men who evinced that spirit. We applauded every suggestion that the young men of Canada don the uniform in order that we who were older might he defended, and we applauded vociferously every man who enlisted. I am not a militarist, any more than any hon. member of this House-not nearly so much, perhaps as some of those who have spoken to-day. But I do feel that as a Canadian I have a duty to perform, not only to Canada but to the British Empire and to the civilized world. I may be asked how it is that we have any militia vote at all when other countries are disarming. But I ask any hon. member to name a country which has not a militia at the present time and is 
not maintaining one? Other countries are disarming to a certain extent, but not any more in proportion than we in Canada are, not any more than we are doing in these estimates.
It is not a question of who is going to gain or lose a few votes. It is not simply a matter of the expenditure of money. This is a question of a real national policy, a policy that affects every man and woman living in Canada to-day, and that will affect their children as well. Do we propose, as a young nation, to shirk the responsibilities of a nation while asking for all the privileges? We asked for a seat in the Genoa Conference; we asked for a seat at the Disarmament Conference at Washington; we asked for a seat at the meeting of the League of Nations; we'asked to be allowed to take part in the formula.	11 p.m. tion of the Versailles treaty;
and now when the time comes that we should maintain our position as a young nation, are we going to shirk, and go back one hundred and fifty years and become Crown colonists to be looked after by Great Britain and not by ourselves? We have a status to maintain as a young people with aspirations, and I must sink my individuality as I believe every member of the House ought to do, in what we might think a little present benefit, because we will be judged as a Dominion in a measure by the part we take as a young nation in the galaxy of nations forming the British Empire and among the nations of the entire world.
I might go on, if it were in order, to mention the navy as well, but I shall leave that until I come to it. We are endeavouring to amalgamate the defence forces of Canada into one department with the object of obtaining efficiency and greater economy, but if the House is to take the attitude that it refuses to grant any money to carry on these services, why amalgamate the defence forces at ail, if we are not going to have any such forces? I do not feel strongly on this question on any personal ground. It makes no difference to me personally whether a dollar is voted, but if we are going to strike out, or reduce to the point where it is practically striking out the item for annual training, we are saying to the young man of Canada and to the boys in the cadet service; we do not want you to be trained any more. We smother your aspirations for getting together to develop your manhood and your physical self, as well as getting your military training.

We have talked a good deal about this to-day, and as we were all up late last night I think we had better rise and think this matter over. I move that the committee rise and report progress.

I notice that the minister did not answer the question I put before. I deprecate the amount of heat that has been brought into this discussion. I think we should discuss these items calmly and dispassionately as Canadians-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would point out to the hon. member that there is a motion before the Chair that the committee rise and report progress. That motion is not debatable.
